Author(s): Hicks, D., Kingsley, G., & Isett, K.R.
Central claim: The paper argues that U.S. state governments respond to the uncertainty of autonomous vehicle technology through two distinct advisory processes: an "expert" mode, in which administrative agencies commission technically credible reports from universities or their own engineering staff, and a "convening" mode, in which political actors such as governors assemble broad stakeholder task forces to build legitimacy for their recommendations.
Gap or limitation: The study can only analyze reports that were findable online, so it likely misses advice generated informally or through channels that were never published, and its measures of legitimacy and credibility are based on report characteristics like length and references rather than on whether the advice changed any actual policy outcome.
Key concepts or framework:
Policy advisory system: the network of committees, agencies, and outside experts that governments draw on to make sense of an emerging technology. 
Salience, legitimacy, and credibility: the three qualities that determine whether knowledge is seen as useful to a policymaker. 
Expert versus convening mode: two contrasting approaches to gathering advice, one prioritizing technical rigor and the other prioritizing broad participation. 
Task force: a stakeholder group assembled by a governor's office to represent multiple interests in a policy report.
Paper Title: Steering the future: expert knowledge and stakeholder voices in autonomous vehicle policy reports
Quotable moment: "The value tends to lie in the engagement, which creates a community of interest" (Discussion, pg 19)
Relevance to argument: This paper directly names the "regulators" our item calls for and shows how even AV policymaking processes explicitly designed to seek public legitimacy still route almost entirely through government officials, consultants, and industry representatives. It is useful evidence that the discourse treats broad "stakeholder engagement" as a matter of assembling the right experts and interest groups, not of consulting the communities the technology will actually operate in.
Synthesis paragraph: Read together, these papers answer our question with striking consistency: engineering and safety-dominant AV discourse centers the people who build, certify, and optimize the machine, and treats everyone else as a factor to be managed. Regulators gather experts rather than communities. Trust becomes a number to fine-tune. Take-over, pedestrian signaling, and traffic flow are all measured for reaction time and road capacity. Even older adults and pedestrians show up mainly as groups to be screened, tracked, or moved along faster. What stands out, though, is not that community need is missing, but that it keeps appearing and then getting turned away. Several studies do touch on the human, relational side of mobility, a rider trusting an operator, a passenger sharing a seat, fairness in who gets picked up, only to fold that insight back into brand acceptance, compliance, or in one case reporting non-compliant road users to the police. The field clearly has the language to treat mobility as a social relationship. It simply chooses not to. That choice is the gap our argument steps into.

Central claim: The paper argues that the one-time safety certification used for conventional vehicles is unsuited to autonomous vehicles, because an AV's competence is not a fixed property of the vehicle but depends heavily on the specific conditions it operates in and continues to change after deployment through software updates; the authors propose regulating AVs more like pharmaceuticals, with staged approval and ongoing post-market monitoring.
Gap or limitation: The drug-approval analogy leaves an important difference unaddressed: a patient consents to take a specific drug, while pedestrians and neighbors who never opted in are exposed to an AV's failure modes, and the paper does not test or validate its proposal against any real regulatory case.
Journal or Proceedings: AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES '18)
Key concepts or framework:
Operational design domain: the specific set of road, weather, and traffic conditions within which an AV is actually competent to drive itself. 
Staged regulatory approval: a phased release process, expanding a system's permitted use only as safety data accumulates, modeled on how new drugs are approved. Post-market surveillance: continuous monitoring of a system's real-world performance after deployment, rather than a single pass or fail test at the outset.
Paper Title: Regulating Autonomous Vehicles: A Policy Proposal
Quotable moment: "Moreover, unlikeclinical drug trials where participants can provide informedconsent, the use of AVs on public roadways will potentiallyaffect many individuals who never gave such consent" (Pros, Cons and Realism, pg 221)
Relevance to argument: This is a clear example of AV governance being framed purely as an engineering-certification problem: the entire proposal is about how regulators can verify a machine is safe, with no discussion of who decides an AV should be deployed in a given community or what purpose it should serve there.

Central claim: The paper argues that the early spread of autonomous vehicle policy across U.S. states is driven mainly by policy learning, meaning states adopt similar rules because they are watching and copying one another and consulting shared intergovernmental organizations and industry groups, rather than because states are competing against each other to attract AV companies.
Gap or limitation: Only 13 of 100 invited officials agreed to be interviewed, a 13 percent response rate, and the statistical model cannot fully separate policy learning from competitive pressure as the actual driving mechanism, a limitation the authors themselves acknowledge.
Key concepts or framework:
Policy diffusion: the process by which a policy innovation spreads from one government to another over time. 
Dyadic event history analysis (DEHA): a statistical method that models pairs of states, one that has adopted a policy and one that has not, to detect which factors predict the second state adopting it too. 
Network governance: the idea that policy decisions emerge from a web of state agencies, private industry, and intergovernmental bodies rather than from a single legislature acting alone.
Paper Title: Policy Learning and the Diffusion of Autonomous Vehicle Policy in the American States
Quotable moment: "While we demonstrate that learning is a key feature of the early spread of this policy innovation, one cannot ignore the growing competitive economic pressures facing the states." (Conclusion)
Relevance to argument: This paper offers a current, well-evidenced picture of AV regulation as an insider conversation among state governments and industry, reinforcing the argument's claim that regulatory discourse names throughput, economic competitiveness, and interstate learning as its central concerns rather than resident or rider need.

Central claim: The paper argues that trust in Level 3 automated vehicles, where control shifts back and forth between the system and the driver, is shaped by six overlapping categories of factors, but that the underlying evidence base is so heavily concentrated in driving simulators and self-report surveys that current knowledge of how trust actually behaves in real-world driving remains limited.
Gap or limitation: The search covered only two databases, ACM Digital Library and Scopus, and was restricted to English-language studies, which the authors acknowledge may exclude relevant interdisciplinary or international research; as a review of existing work, it also cannot generate any new evidence beyond what the underlying 80 studies already found.
Journal or Proceedings: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting, 69(1), 1281-1283
Key concepts or framework:
Trust calibration: the idea that a driver's trust should match the automation's true competence, neither too high nor too low. 
PRISMA-guided review: a standardized method for searching, screening, and selecting studies for inclusion in a systematic review, used here to identify 80 eligible papers. 
Ecological validity: the extent to which findings from a controlled study, such as one run in a driving simulator, would hold up in real-world conditions.
Paper Title: Trust in Level 3 Automated Vehicles: A Systematic Literature Review
Quotable moment: "The review also revealed that research on trust in L3 driving remains largely confined to controlled environments, with 92.5% of studies conducted in simulators and only 7.5% in real-world settings." (Outcome, pg 3)
Relevance to argument: This review provides recent, comprehensive evidence for the argument's claim that trust is treated as an individually measured psychological variable rather than a socially or relationally built property, and its own finding that over 90 percent of studies rely on simulators and surveys underscores how narrow the field's methods are.

Central claim: The paper argues that consumers' trust in self-driving vehicles can be reverse-engineered from the open-ended comments attached to their survey ratings, and that because almost no respondent has actually ridden in one, this trust rests on societal and relational expectations, of manufacturers, brands, and government safety assurance, rather than on any direct experience of the vehicle itself.
Gap or limitation: Every respondent was a driver who had never experienced a self-driving vehicle and was therefore forced to imagine it, and the authors concede that availability bias, demographic variation, and the assumption that measured attitudes predict behavior all limit the findings, with availability, privacy, and fairness explicitly set aside as less salient than safety.
Journal or Proceedings: Human Factors: The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society, 62(2), 260-277
Key concepts or framework:
Structural topic modeling (STM): a text-analysis method that treats words as data to surface recurring themes across thousands of open-ended comments, while letting outside variables such as the trust rating and survey year shift which themes appear. 
Dread risk: a heightened, disproportionate sense of risk attached to hazards that feel uncontrollable, unobservable, and catastrophic, which can depress trust regardless of a system's actual safety record. 
Disappointment, violation, and betrayal: three escalating readings of an automation failure, a mundane performance lapse, a broken social norm, or a fundamental breach of purpose, with the latter two doing far more damage to trust. 
Societal and relational trust: trust borrowed from expectations about institutions and from experience with analogous technologies, leaned on when a person has no direct experience of the system itself.
Paper Title: Exploring Trust in Self-Driving Vehicles Through Text Analysis
Quotable moment:
"For example, the algorithms for sending a vehicle to pick up a passenger might be unfair and biased toward certain socioeconomic groups, similar to the
biases that have emerged in Uber’s ride request algorithms (Hanrahan, Ma, & Yuan, 2017), and algorithms more generally (Courtland, 2018)." (Limitations and Generalization, pg 16)
Relevance to argument: This is a strong trust-in-automation anchor because it treats trust as something to be reverse-engineered from consumer ratings so that manufacturers can cultivate acceptance, reinforcing the argument's claim that the field measures trust as an individual attitude to be managed. Notably, it surfaces the very relational and societal bases of trust our thread cares about, then routes them back toward brand and manufacturer strategy rather than community authority. In its own limitations it even concedes that the algorithms dispatching a vehicle to a passenger may be biased against certain socioeconomic groups, but files this under future concerns less salient than safety.

Author(s): Kraus, J., Scholz, D., Stiegemeier, D., & Baumann, M.
Central claim: The paper argues that a driver's trust in an automated vehicle is a dynamic quantity continuously recalibrated in a feedback loop as the system performs: it climbs steadily during error-free driving, dips temporarily after take-overs and malfunctions, recovers as error-free operation resumes, and can be shielded from that dip altogether by giving the driver transparent information about the system's limitations beforehand.
Gap or limitation: The studies ran in a low-risk simulator with young, mostly student samples experiencing only single, mild malfunctions, and the authors concede that real-world risk, repeated or high-consequence malfunctions, and behavioral rather than self-reported trust measures all remain untested; nothing in the design speaks to riders who never take control.
Journal or Proceedings: Human Factors: The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society, 62(5), 718-736
Key concepts or framework:
Trust calibration: matching a driver's level of trust to the automation's actual capabilities so the driver neither over-relies (misuse) nor under-relies (disuse) on the system. 
Dynamic trust model and updating feedback loop: the authors' framework in which trust is continuously revised as expectations formed before the drive are compared against the system's observed behavior during it. 
Take-over request (TOR): the system's handback of control to the driver when it reaches a condition it was not designed to handle. 
System transparency: how much a system discloses about its own limits and likely failures, here as advance information that inoculates trust against the shock of a malfunction.
Paper Title: The More You Know: Trust Dynamics and Calibration in Highly Automated Driving and the Effects of Take-Overs, System Malfunction, and System Transparency
Quotable moment: "At the same time, an understanding of these processes seems important, as calibrated trust may serve as a benchmark for safe and efficient design of driving automation and the associated interaction strategies in terms of information provided prior to (tutorials, user guides, marketing, and training) and during system use (human-machine interface [HMI] concepts)." (Introduction, pg 719)
Relevance to argument: This is a paradigmatic trust-in-automation anchor: trust is operationalized as a repeatedly measured scalar and framed explicitly as a benchmark for safe and efficient design, supporting the argument's claim that the discourse treats trust as an engineering control variable to be calibrated rather than a relational, accountability-based bond. It complements Lee and Kolodge by supplying the in-vehicle, simulator-based experimental version of the same reduction.

Author(s): Zhang, B., de Winter, J., Varotto, S., Happee, R., & Martens, M.
Central claim: The paper argues that drivers do not take over control from an automated vehicle as quickly as they are physically able to; instead, take-over time is shaped mainly by the urgency of the situation, the modality of the alert, and prior experience with take-overs, while handling a handheld device during automated driving substantially slows the response.
Gap or limitation: All 129 included studies were conducted with ordinary working-age adult drivers, almost entirely in simulators rather than on real roads, so the meta-analysis has no data on elderly drivers, disabled drivers, or non-drivers, and it measures take-over time only, not whether the resulting maneuver was actually a safe one.
Journal or Proceedings: Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour, 64, 285-307
Key concepts or framework:
Take-over time (TOT): the interval between the onset of a take-over request or a critical event and the moment the driver actually intervenes. 
Meta-analysis: a statistical technique for combining results across many separate studies to identify overall patterns, here using three complementary methods. 
Non-driving related task (NDRT): any secondary activity, such as reading or using a phone, that a driver engages in while the vehicle drives itself. 
Time budget: the amount of time available before a hazard must be addressed.
Paper Title: Determinants of take-over time from automated driving: A meta-analysis of 129 studies
Quotable moment: "The use of a handheld device strongly increased the mean TOT" (Results, Pg 12)
Relevance to argument: As the most comprehensive quantitative synthesis in the take-over literature, this paper is strong evidence for how the field's core vocabulary, time budgets, urgency levels, and take-over quality, is built entirely around efficiency and safety-margin optimization rather than around the purpose or context of the trip being taken.

Author(s): Peng, Q., Wu, Y., Qie, N., & Iwaki, S.
Central claim: The paper argues that older drivers' weaker performance after a take-over request is better explained by specific executive-function abilities, particularly the ability to shift between tasks and update working memory, than by chronological age itself.
Gap or limitation: The driving task used a desktop simulator rather than a higher-fidelity setup, so part of the measured correlation between cognitive scores and driving performance may reflect general comfort with computer-based tasks rather than driving ability specifically, and the sample of 70 participants was drawn from a single Japanese city, limiting how broadly the findings generalize.
Key concepts or framework:
Executive function: a set of higher-order cognitive control processes, broken down here into updating, inhibition, and shifting, each measured through a dedicated computerized task. 
Principal component analysis (PCA): a statistical technique that distills many separate test scores into a smaller number of underlying cognitive components. 
Take-over performance: operationalized in this study as the steadiness of steering after a take-over request and the time-to-collision at the moment of a lane change.
Paper Title: Age-related effects of executive function on takeover performance in automated driving
Quotable moment: "Similarly, our findings can guide quick screening for elderly drivers’ cognitive status for a TOR of highly automated vehicles, such as an exam for elderly drivers’ license updating, or a lite system monitoring the cognitive status of elderly drivers." (Application)
Relevance to argument: This is the sub-theme's paper most directly relevant to an aging population: it treats older adults' relationship with automated vehicles almost entirely as a safety and cognitive-performance question to be measured and screened, illustrating how even research focused on an underserved group still frames that group through an engineering-safety lens rather than a service or relational one.

Central claim: The paper argues that no single external human-machine interface design is best for every purpose: text-based displays give pedestrians the clearest understanding of a vehicle's intent, light-bar signals produce the fastest reaction time, and designs that convey a vehicle's actual yielding intent consistently outperform designs that only show whether the vehicle is in automated mode.
Gap or limitation: The search was restricted to studies published in the last five years and written in English, and it explicitly excluded video-based, non-immersive studies, so it may miss earlier foundational work; nearly every included study also tested only a single pedestrian crossing in front of a single vehicle, leaving open how these signals would perform with multiple pedestrians or vehicles present at once.
Journal or Proceedings: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting, 69(1), 1198-1203
Key concepts or framework:
External human-machine interface (eHMI): any external signal, text, icon, light bar, or projection, that an automated vehicle uses to communicate with pedestrians in place of a driver's eye contact or hand gestures. 
Static versus dynamic eHMI: a static display shows only the vehicle's automation state, while a dynamic display conveys richer, situation-specific information such as yielding intent. 
Crossing initiation time (CIT): how quickly a pedestrian begins to cross after seeing a signal, the field's primary safety and efficiency outcome measure.
Paper Title: Where to Look? A Review of External Autonomous Vehicle Signaling to Increase Pedestrian Safety
Quotable moment:
"While visual eHMI concepts have numerous demonstrated
benefits to pedestrian crossing and safety, one drawback is
that the user must be looking at the interface to derive its
meaning." (Results, pg 1200)
Relevance to argument: As a 2025 update to the interaction-level AV literature, this review confirms that even the newest external-communication research remains organized entirely around signal design and crossing-time optimization, supporting the argument's claim that AV-pedestrian interaction is framed as a communication-design problem rather than a question of community access or consent.

Author(s): Lee, M.B., Lee, C.T., Abas, M.A., & Chong, W.W.F.
Central claim: The paper argues that research on autonomous vehicles and pedestrian safety, based on a bibliometric analysis of 368 publications from 2013 to 2023, clusters into three main areas, behavioral and interaction studies, collision-avoidance technology, and statistical risk analysis, but that the field's heavy reliance on controlled tests leaves policymakers without the real-world evidence needed to write effective regulations.
Gap or limitation: Because a bibliometric analysis only counts and maps existing publications, it cannot evaluate whether the most-cited studies actually reached correct or generalizable conclusions, only that they were widely read and cited, so it offers no independent evidence about pedestrian experience or need.
Journal or Proceedings: Journal of Traffic and Transportation Engineering (English Edition), 12(4), 772-794
Key concepts or framework:
Bibliometric analysis: a quantitative method for mapping a research field by studying patterns of publication, citation, and co-citation rather than reading each paper individually. 
Co-citation network: a map of which journals or papers tend to be cited together, revealing how different parts of a field relate to one another. 
Research cluster: a group of thematically related studies identified through the bibliometric mapping process.
Paper Title: Advancing pedestrian safety in the era of autonomous vehicles: A bibliometric analysis and pathway to effective regulations
Quotable moment: "Pedestrians account for 54% of the annual road traffic death toll of over 1.35 million fatalities (World Health Organization, 2018)." (Introduction)
Relevance to argument: This paper offers a bird's-eye confirmation of the argument's central claim from a different angle: even mapped across the entire published literature, AV-pedestrian safety research is dominated by engineering and statistical approaches, with policy explicitly named as an underdeveloped area still catching up to the technology.

Author(s): Kooijman, L., Happee, R., & de Winter, J.C.F.
Central claim: The paper argues that when pedestrians are allowed to actually step into the road instead of merely imagining it, the presence of an eHMI on a yielding vehicle measurably speeds up their crossing, prompting them to leave the curb sooner and walk faster, with a text display outperforming front brake lights, and that a head-mounted display paired with a full-body motion suit can read a pedestrian's crossing intention directly from body motion in ways surveys and button-presses cannot.
Gap or limitation: The study ran with only 24 mostly young, student participants in a controlled single-pedestrian, single-crossing virtual scene with no real traffic, no bidirectional flows, and no other pedestrians, and the authors concede a scripting error forced them to drop one condition and that the motion suit added usability problems without clearly improving immersion, leaving open how these signals behave in genuinely complex, shared, community traffic.
Key concepts or framework:
External human-machine interface (eHMI): an external signal on a vehicle, here a text display reading "walk"/"don't walk" or front brake lights, meant to replace the driver's cues and tell a pedestrian whether it is safe to cross. 
Objective versus subjective crossing measures: the paper's distinction between what pedestrians say (survey ratings, button presses) and what their bodies do (forward gait velocity, moment of leaving the curb, thorax angle), captured here with motion sensors. 
Forward gait velocity as a safety index: the assumption that faster forward walking signals a pedestrian's perceived safety, used as the study's main objective outcome. 
Perceptual fidelity: how closely a given method (survey, VR headset, motion suit, field test) reproduces a real crossing, which the paper treats as the key axis for choosing how to evaluate eHMIs.
Paper Title: How Do eHMIs Affect Pedestrians' Crossing Behavior? A Study Using a Head-Mounted Display Combined with a Motion Suit
Quotable moment: "Additionally, the 3D recording of pedestrians in crossing situations could be beneficial to perception and modeling research (e.g., [40,41]), where the goal is to have self-driving vehicles detecting the posture of pedestrians and infer their crossing intention." (Discussion, future research)
Relevance to argument: This is a strong external-HMI anchor because it treats the pedestrian encounter purely as a signal-legibility and crossing-speed optimization problem, extending the field's usual survey and button methods into full-body motion capture so that crossing intention can be read off the body itself, supporting the argument's claim that AV-pedestrian interaction is framed as a communication-design problem measured in reaction time and gait rather than a question of who has standing to shape the street. Its closing suggestion that vehicles could detect pedestrians' posture to infer their intent shows the same instrument turned toward surveillance of the road user.

Author(s): Pimenta, A.R., Kamruzzaman, M., & Currie, G.
Central claim: The paper argues that autonomous vehicles will reshape cities unevenly depending on how they are owned and operated: shared autonomous vehicles tend to free up parking and support denser, more efficient city centers, while privately owned autonomous vehicles tend to encourage urban sprawl and lower-density suburban growth.
Gap or limitation: The review explicitly notes that no reviewed study considered whether parking land freed up by autonomous vehicles could be intentionally redirected toward community-defined uses such as affordable housing, rather than left to market-driven redevelopment; it also excludes autonomous mass transit and aerial taxis, narrowing which built-environment effects it can address.
Key concepts or framework:
Causal loop diagram (CLD): a visual method for mapping cause-and-effect relationships and feedback loops between variables such as parking demand, density, and accessibility. 
Shared versus private autonomous vehicles (SAV/PAV): the two dominant ownership and operating models the review compares throughout. 
Empty-cruising: an autonomous vehicle driving without passengers, either searching for free parking or returning to a base, which affects congestion and land use. 
Built environment: the physical, human-made features of a city, including parking, density, land use mix, and street design.
Paper Title: Long-term effects of autonomous vehicles on the built environment: a systematic scoping review towards conceptual frameworks
Quotable moment: "For example,SAVs may likely contribute to increasing residential and employment densities in the CBD" (Conclusion, Pg 1107 )
Relevance to argument: As a comprehensive and recent throughput and urban-planning anchor, this review shows that even the most holistic synthesis of autonomous vehicle effects on cities still frames the built environment as something engineered and forecast from above, never as something a community actively shapes.

Author(s): Park, J., Jang, S., & Ko, J.
Central claim: The paper argues that converting a regular expressway lane into an autonomous-vehicle-exclusive lane only improves traffic efficiency once autonomous vehicles make up roughly 20 to 30 percent of all traffic; below that threshold, the exclusive lane sits underused while human-driven traffic is squeezed into fewer lanes, worsening congestion.
Gap or limitation: The authors acknowledge that their model assumes current travel patterns stay fixed and does not account for new trips people might make once autonomous vehicles are available, including trips by people who could not previously drive; the capacity-gain figures are also borrowed from a U.S. engineering manual that may not fully reflect Korean road conditions.
Key concepts or framework:
Market penetration rate (MPR): the percentage of vehicles on the road that are autonomous, the study's key threshold variable. 
Capacity gain: the increase in road throughput that autonomous vehicles enable through shorter following distances and faster reaction times. 
Vehicle-kilometers traveled (VKT) and total time spent (TTS): the two primary traffic-performance metrics tracked in the simulation.
Paper Title: Effects of Exclusive Lanes for Autonomous Vehicles on Urban Expressways under Mixed Traffic of Autonomous and Human-Driven Vehicles
Quotable moment: "This study suggests that the introduction of AV-exclusive lanes cannot be guaranteed to be effective at MPR levels below 20 to 30%, given the assumed capacity gains provided by HCM. (Results and Discussion section)
Relevance to argument: This is a clean, current example of throughput optimization as the field's guiding logic: the entire study is organized around the question of at what percentage of adoption a policy maximizes network efficiency, with no reference to who is traveling or for what purpose.

Author(s): Lu, Q., Tettamanti, T., Hörcher, D., & Varga, I.
Central claim: The paper argues that raising the share of autonomous vehicles lifts an urban road network's capacity in a roughly linear way, by about 16% in a simulated grid network and about 24% in a real Budapest network at full automation, because autonomous vehicles keep shorter headways and react faster, and it offers a generalized additive model for fitting the macroscopic fundamental diagram at any penetration rate.
Gap or limitation: The study models only capacity under fixed, simulated demand with no connected-vehicle communication, and says nothing about who travels, why, or whether higher throughput translates into access; the authors also note their gains fall below some prior single-intersection estimates because network-level vehicle accumulation was included, underlining that the analysis is purely a flow-optimization exercise.
Journal or Proceedings: Transportation Letters: The International Journal of Transportation Research, 12(8), 540-549
Key concepts or framework:
Macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD): a network-level model relating traffic flow, vehicle density, and average speed, used here as the basic description of a road network's capacity. 
Market penetration rate: the share of vehicles on the network that are autonomous, stepped from 0% to 100% as the study's main independent variable. 
Headway and reaction time: the following distance and response delay between vehicles; because autonomous vehicles are modeled with shorter, faster values, they push more flow through the same road.
 Generalized additive model (GAM): a semiparametric regression the authors use to fit the speed-density relationship without assuming its exact shape, then convert it into the flow-density curve.
Paper Title: The impact of autonomous vehicles on urban traffic network capacity: an experimental analysis by microscopic traffic simulation
Quotable moment: "The paper investigates the impactsof AVs, with a special spotlight on the eﬃciency of utilizing theexisting infrastructure, namely, the capacity of the road network. (Introduction, pg 540)
Relevance to argument: This is a clean, current throughput anchor: its stated goal is the efficiency of utilizing existing infrastructure, and its entire contribution is a capacity percentage recovered from simulated flow, with humans present only as vehicle counts, supporting the argument's claim that the field measures the value of automated mobility as network throughput rather than as who is served or for what purpose. It even opens by framing new road construction as too costly and instead prizes extracting more capacity from the roads already there, never asking whom that recovered capacity is for.

Author(s): Palatinus, Z., Volosin, M., Csabi, E., Hallgato, E., Hajnal, E., Lukovics, M., Pronay, S., Ujhazi, T., Osztobanyi, L., Szabo, B., Kralik, T., & Majo-Petri, Z.
Central claim: The paper argues that riding in a genuinely self-driving vehicle produces measurably different brain and eye-movement patterns than riding with a human driver, showing less positive emotional affect on EEG measures during the autonomous condition even though overall alertness remained similarly high, suggesting people respond to autonomous vehicles with physiological caution that goes beyond what they report in surveys.
Gap or limitation: The authors describe the study as an exploratory pilot, and the same ride order, human-driven first, then autonomous, was used for every participant rather than being randomized, so an order effect may account for some of the reported differences, a limitation the authors note directly.
Key concepts or framework:
Frontal alpha asymmetry: an EEG measure comparing left and right frontal brain activity, used here as an index of positive versus negative emotional orientation. 
Multifractal spectrum width: a complexity measure derived from eye-tracking data indicating how many distinct underlying processes are shaping a person's eye movements. 
UTAUT2 (Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology): the standard survey-based technology-acceptance framework the study aims to supplement with physiological rather than purely self-reported data.
Paper Title: Physiological measurements in social acceptance of self driving technologies
Quotable moment: "We found an overall narrower MF spectrum width in the Autonomous condition. Regarding EEG, frontal alpha asymmetry values were higher in the Human condition compared to the Autonomous condition, while arousal levels did not differ between the two conditions." (Discussion)
Relevance to argument: As one of relatively few studies placing real riders in a real, moving autonomous vehicle rather than a simulator, this paper is a methodologically distinct anchor for the acceptance sub-theme, but it still frames acceptance as an individual, measurable affective state rather than something built through a familiar or trusted service relationship.

Author(s): Zoellick, J.C., Kuhlmey, A., Schenk, L., Schindel, D., & Bluher, S.
Central claim: The paper argues that while 125 real riders surveyed immediately after an actual ride in a shared electric autonomous shuttle reported high acceptance, trust, and intention to use, the researchers' own statistical tests show that the standard survey scales used across the field to measure these attitudes do not hold together as cleanly as assumed, raising doubts about what prior acceptance research has actually been measuring.
Gap or limitation: The sample was self-selected, young, and drawn from visitors to a public science event riding a slow, twelve kilometer-per-hour shuttle on private land with a safety operator aboard, and the authors themselves caution against generalizing beyond this specific group or to sustained, repeated use over time.
Key concepts or framework:
Technology acceptance constructs: the standard set of attitude measures, including acceptance, trust, perceived safety, and intention to use, adapted from general technology-acceptance research and applied here to autonomous vehicles. 
Construct validity: whether a survey scale genuinely measures the distinct concept it claims to, tested here through factor analysis. 
Hypothetical bias: the concern that people's stated attitudes toward autonomous vehicles in an imagined scenario may not reflect how they would actually feel after real exposure.
Paper Title: Assessing acceptance of electric automated vehicles after exposure in a realistic traffic environment
Quotable moment: "Participants accepted and trusted the electric AVs, perceived them as safe, and intended to use one in the future. Participants were amused, surprised, and not afraid after the ride with an electric AV. (Summary)
Relevance to argument: This paper is a strong methodological complement to Palatinus et al., offering real riders in realistic though low-speed conditions rather than a simulator, and its qualitative finding that a human safety operator meaningfully shaped riders' perceptions is a rare moment in this literature where a rider's relational experience of the ride surfaces at all, even though the researchers treat it as a confounding variable to control for rather than something to design around.

Author(s): Nordhoff, S., Stapel, J., van Arem, B., & Happee, R.
Central claim: The paper argues that passengers' perceived safety in a driverless shuttle is assembled from concrete vehicle- and environment-level cues, low speed, smooth braking, the emergency button, operation on a controlled route, and that the successful integration of automated shuttles therefore depends on engineering these perceptions and on managing how outside pedestrians and cyclists interact with the vehicle.
Gap or limitation: Passengers only imagined interacting with the shuttle as pedestrians or cyclists rather than actually doing so, the vehicle ran slowly on a controlled private campus with a hidden steward aboard, and the sample was self-selected from mobility-project and meetup participants, so the authors caution that perceived safety in faster, genuinely driverless, mixed-traffic conditions remains untested.
Journal or Proceedings: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice, 138, 508-524
Key concepts or framework:
Perceived safety: a passenger's subjective feeling of safety, distinct from actual safety, decomposed here into vehicle-, individual-, and environment-related factors and treated as the central precondition for acceptance. 
Hidden safety steward: a human operator disguised as a 'minute writer' so riders experience the shuttle as genuinely driverless, keeping the study's safety net from inflating perceived safety. 
Incidental or vulnerable road users: pedestrians and cyclists who never chose to interact with the shuttle but must negotiate it anyway, whose acceptance the paper treats as a second necessary condition for deployment. 
Testing behavior: the tendency of passengers to press the emergency button and of outside road users to step in front of the shuttle to probe its limits, which the paper reads as distrust, curiosity, or a problem to be managed.
Paper Title: Passenger opinions of the perceived safety and interaction with automated shuttles: A test ride study with 'hidden' safety steward
Quotable moment: "Manufacturers, vehicle operators, and the media should educate the public that the testing of automated vehicles could jeopardize the safety and efficiency benefits of vehicle automation." (Discussion, sec. 4.2)
Relevance to argument: This is the acceptance sub-theme's most community-adjacent anchor, real riders in a real moving vehicle, whose relational cues such as sharing the ride and trusting a responsible transport operator briefly surface, yet it still frames the whole encounter as perceived safety to be optimized for successful deployment. Its remedies for road users who negotiate with the shuttle run toward educating them, redesigning the vehicle for compliance, or sanctioning them, rather than accommodating their needs, showing exactly where the mainstream approaches a service or relational framing and then turns back.

Central claim: Disabled transit riders in Austin and Seattle face similar first and last mile barriers despite different transit systems and geographies, shaped by intersectionality, social context, built environment quality, confidence, and relationships with public agencies. Disabled voices are systematically excluded from planning, perpetuating inequitable outcomes.
Gap or limitation: The sample was recruited through advocacy networks and email, skewing toward riders already engaged with accessibility issues and excluding disabled people without internet access.
Key concepts or framework: Mobility justice: multi-scalar framework examining how the built environment reproduces privilege and power beyond basic accessibility. First and last mile: trip segments connecting riders to fixed transit, where accessibility gaps concentrate. Intersectionality: overlapping identities shaping distinct travel burdens.
Paper Title: "The bus is accessible, but how do you get to the bus": First and last mile experiences of disabled transit riders
Quotable moment: "The bus is accessible, but how do you get to the bus?" (p. 5).
Relevance to argument: Supports both halves of the claim. Mobility access is unevenly distributed by disability type, gender, and race even in cities with strong accessibility investment, and infrastructure built to minimum ADA standards without disabled riders' participation reproduces exclusion along the first and last mile. Participants report being seldom in the room when transportation decisions are made, and describe the active transportation engagement process itself as white and male dominated.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper grounds both the uneven distribution and exclusion-from-participation claims in first-person accounts, showing that even accessibility-focused cities produce disproportionate travel burdens when planners ignore first and last mile segments and exclude disabled riders from decision-making. It argues meaningful engagement, not compliance alone, is necessary for equitable mobility infrastructure.

Central claim: A systematic review of 138 papers finds the elderly experience the highest inequality in public transport resource distribution among disadvantaged traveler groups. It synthesizes a four part framework, opportunity accessibility, physical accessibility, age friendly informationalization, and cost affordability, for transport inclusion policy.
Gap or limitation: The evaluation framework assumes public transit dependent cities and fits poorly in car dependent or rural contexts, and it pools evidence on other disadvantaged groups without a participatory method to test the framework directly.
Journal or Proceedings: Journal of Traffic and Transportation Engineering (English Edition), 11(2), 312-347
Key concepts or framework: Transport related social exclusion: marginalization from daily activities caused by inadequate transport across accessibility, physical, information, and economic dimensions. Capability approach: evaluates inclusion by whether services convert into real capabilities. Spatial production theory: transport spaces shape perceived social inclusion.
Paper Title: Public transport inclusion and active aging: A systematic review on elderly mobility
Quotable moment: "the elderly have the highest level of inequality in PT resource distribution" (p. 2).
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half directly, documenting that elderly people face the highest transport resource inequality among disadvantaged groups across three decades of research. It does not address community participation in infrastructure decisions: its own framework is top down and metric driven, built from published literature rather than elderly travelers' input, making it a thinner fit for the infrastructure without participation half of the claim.
Synthesis paragraph: This review documents that elderly people face the steepest transport inequality among disadvantaged groups, giving quantitative backing to the claim that mobility access has long been unevenly distributed. Its own accessibility centered framework, however, is built from literature rather than elderly voices, illustrating by contrast why participatory approaches matter for defining what inclusion requires.

Central claim: California's community transportation needs assessment pilot program, intended to include historically underrepresented groups in transportation planning, largely reproduced the same representation gaps and engagement shortfalls as traditional public participation processes.
Gap or limitation: The study cannot confirm whether any assessment's recommendations changed actual transportation plans or funding, and it analyzes only California's pilot program, limiting generalizability to other participatory models.
Key concepts or framework: Community transportation needs assessment: a grassroots funded study meant to engage underrepresented residents in identifying transportation needs. Representation gap: participants in planning processes skew older, whiter, and more affluent than the community. Tokenism: participation that solicits input without incorporating it into decisions.
Paper Title: Bridging the gap: Do community needs assessments enhance public participation in transportation planning?
Quotable moment: "urban renewal projects of the 1950s and 1960s that displaced more than 1 million Americans, residents that were disproportionately low-income and Black" (p. 2).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half of the claim. It shows that even funded, explicitly inclusive community needs assessments replicate historic representation gaps rather than closing them, and traces this pattern back to the 1950s and 1960s highway projects that displaced low income and Black residents with little say in the process.
Synthesis paragraph: Even when agencies fund grassroots, explicitly inclusive needs assessments, this study finds they largely reproduce the same representation gaps as traditional public meetings. It underscores that participation structures, not just their existence, determine whether infrastructure decisions genuinely include disadvantaged communities, grounding the section's exclusion claim in a contemporary case rather than only historical precedent.

Central claim: Interviews with Canadian transportation advocates identify four ways that mobility planning tools and information systems deepen the divide between planners and the public. Path dependence in transportation knowledge infrastructures is a systemic barrier to overcoming these mobility injustices.
Gap or limitation: The sample is limited to advocacy organizations already engaged in mobility justice work in Canada, so it may not capture residents who never reach an advocacy organization at all.
Key concepts or framework: Mobility justice: Sheller's framework analyzing interacting relations of movement, dividing populations into kinetic elite and mobility poor. Path dependence: how the historical design of planning tools locks in and perpetuates exclusion. Data infrastructure literacy: sensitivity to the social and political contexts data is embedded in.
Paper Title: Moving Towards Mobility Justice: Challenges and Considerations for Supporting Advocacy
Quotable moment: "a conversation that only some people are allowed to be in" (p. 8).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. Advocates describe how technically inaccessible tools, English only materials, and planners' hyper focus on traffic counts over lived experience shut residents out of decisions, echoing the historical divide between the kinetic elite and the mobility poor that mobility justice scholarship names.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper grounds the exclusion half of the claim in current advocacy work, showing that technical jargon, English only materials, and planners' narrow traffic metrics reproduce the same divide between decision makers and residents that mobility justice scholarship critiques historically. It introduces path dependence as a mechanism for why exclusionary infrastructure persists.

Central claim: Three co-creation focus groups with institutional, technical, and citizen actors in a low-density Portuguese suburb produced eight collaboratively defined mobility strategies spanning pedestrian and cycling infrastructure, transit reliability, and governance. Accessibility, inclusiveness, and institutional coordination emerge as interdependent conditions for equitable mobility transitions.
Gap or limitation: The case draws on a single suburb and a limited number of focus groups skewed toward older participants, so the strategies are preliminary and unvalidated against underrepresented groups' needs.
Key concepts or framework: 15-Minute City, Transit-Oriented Development, and Mobility as a Service: proximity based planning paradigms reinterpreted by participants as functional access goals rather than fixed density templates. Co-creation: focus group based collective strategy building across institutional, technical, and citizen stakeholders.
Paper Title: Co-Creating Accessibility-Centred Mobility Strategies in Low-Density Suburban Contexts: Evidence from Coimbra, Portugal
Quotable moment: "key to rebuilding trust in public transport" (p. 22).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half, showing that treating proximity-based models like the 15-Minute City and TOD as co-created rather than fixed templates surfaces needs, such as trust in transit reliability and safe pedestrian access, that top down planning alone would miss.
Synthesis paragraph: This case shows that participatory reinterpretation of proximity based planning models, rather than top down application, is what surfaces suburban residents' actual priorities, though the strategies here reflect mostly older adults and remain unvalidated. It offers a concrete example of co-creation as a mechanism for avoiding exclusionary infrastructure.

Central claim: Surveys of transportation professionals and the public reveal an Arnstein Gap, a persistent difference between the public involvement stakeholders experience and what they want in transportation infrastructure planning. The paper proposes structured public involvement, using geovisual decision support tools, to narrow this gap without requiring full consensus.
Gap or limitation: The survey based Arnstein Gap metric captures perceived involvement levels but not whether structured public involvement deployments change actual infrastructure outcomes, and the case studies are limited to a handful of U.S. states.
Journal or Proceedings: Annals of the Association of American Geographers, 100(1), 57-86
Key concepts or framework: Arnstein Gap: the measured difference between perceived and desired public involvement on Arnstein's ladder of citizen participation. Structured public involvement: a reflexive, nonconsensual framework using geovisual tools to elicit and respect community cultural values. Procedural justice: attaining spatial justice through fair process rather than fair distribution alone.
Paper Title: Toward Structured Public Involvement: Justice, Geography and Collaborative Geospatial/Geovisual Decision Support Systems
Quotable moment: "The Arnstein Gap indicates that the public desire a TI planning and design system that is more directly responsive to public needs" (p. 7).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. The Arnstein Gap quantifies a persistent, measured shortfall in transportation infrastructure decision making that professionals do not fully recognize, and the paper argues this gap is structural to U.S. transportation planning rather than an occasional failure.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper offers historical and methodological grounding for why participation gaps in infrastructure planning persist, showing empirically that professionals underestimate the disconnect between desired and actual public involvement. It supports treating infrastructure without participation as a structural, measurable problem, and frames a participatory alternative that need not require full consensus to be legitimate.

Central claim: Twenty interviews with disabled people in Montreal and a conceptual counter-cartography approach show that dominant definitions of active travel, limited to biking and walking on foot, exclude wheelchair, scooter, and adapted cycle users. The paper argues infrastructure should center disability justice and disabled people's leadership rather than retrofit universal design standards.
Gap or limitation: The study draws on 20 interviews in a single city, and the authors call for broader research across more disability communities to inform infrastructural design processes.
Key concepts or framework: Counter-cartography: a mapping method layering policy definitions against interview accounts to expose whose mobility practices get excluded. Disability justice: a framework centering disabled people's leadership, distinct from accommodation focused universal design. Crip time: reframing infrastructure to bend to disabled bodies' pace rather than the reverse.
Paper Title: Centering disability justice in active transportation transitions: A conceptual counter-cartography
Quotable moment: "sidewalks hit hard" (p. 6).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. Montreal's own policy definitions of active travel exclude many disabled people's actual mobility practices, and interviewees describe cycling infrastructure too narrow for tricycles and adapted cycles, showing how planning built without disabled people's input structurally forecloses their access.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper shows that official definitions of active travel, not just physical infrastructure, can foreclose disabled people's access, since Montreal's own policy language excludes many disabled mobility practices before infrastructure is even built. It reinforces that centering disabled people's expertise and leadership, not only accommodation, is necessary for genuinely inclusive infrastructure decisions.

Central claim: Interviews with 28 Black and people of color transportation professionals in California distinguish performative equity work, which privileges dominant groups' comfort and produces only superficial change, from authentic equity work, which redistributes decision making power and produces measurable change for historically oppressed communities.
Gap or limitation: The study is limited to California and did not achieve representation from Indigenous or tribal transportation professionals despite specific recruitment efforts, limiting the framework's tested scope.
Key concepts or framework: Performative equity work: actions or rhetoric that claim to address equity without materially changing outcomes or power. Authentic equity work: sustained redistribution of funding, time, and decision making power to affected communities. Arrested mobility: policing practices that apprehend or harm Black people simply for moving through public space.
Paper Title: Performative versus Authentic Equity Work: An Assessment of Current Practices in Transportation Planning
Quotable moment: "Many communities know the solutions to the challenges they face" (p. 12).
Relevance to argument: Supports both halves of the claim. It documents uneven distribution of power and voice among transportation professionals of color within the field itself, and argues that infrastructure and funding decisions made without genuinely redistributing power to communities, not just consulting them, reproduce the same exclusion regardless of stated equity commitments.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper reframes community participation as insufficient unless paired with actual redistribution of power and resources, showing that even self identified equity conscious agencies can produce only performative change. It supports the section's exclusion claim by locating the same power imbalance inside the transportation profession itself, not only in public facing planning processes.

Central claim: A deep learning analysis of infrastructure expenditure and social vulnerability across 394 US municipalities finds infrastructure investment inequality increased from 2010 to 2019 in nearly every sector, and that shifting from population based to equity centered funding allocation would measurably reduce socioeconomic vulnerability.
Gap or limitation: The model treats infrastructure categories broadly without distinguishing transportation modes, relies on a black box machine learning approach whose internal relationships are hard to interpret, and by the authors' own account still needs community-driven qualitative input.
Key concepts or framework: Social Vulnerability Index: a CDC composite measure of socioeconomic disadvantage used to track which municipalities are underserved. Equality centered versus equity centered allocation: distributing infrastructure funds evenly per capita versus targeting funds toward the most vulnerable municipalities.
Paper Title: Assessing equity in infrastructure investment distribution among U.S. cities
Quotable moment: "fosters community engagement and ownership, leading to further improvements in the equitable decision-making process" (p. 11).
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half directly, quantifying growing infrastructure investment inequality across a decade and showing which municipalities are shortchanged. It is a thinner fit for the participation half: the framework is data driven and top down, and the authors themselves flag the need to pair it with community engagement to make decisions genuinely equitable.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper offers strong quantitative evidence that infrastructure investment inequality has been widening and that equity centered allocation would help close it, reinforcing the section's uneven distribution claim. It is honest about its own limits, though: as a purely data driven model, it cannot substitute for the community engagement the section argues infrastructure decisions actually require.

Central claim: A 2005 civil rights lawsuit against the Bay Area's Metropolitan Transportation Commission reveals that race neutral regional transit funding, favoring suburban rail expansion over Oakland bus service, reproduced a racialized geography built by decades of earlier overt housing and employment discrimination.
Gap or limitation: The analysis focuses on one metropolitan region and one legal case, and does not evaluate whether newer transit oriented development plans in Priority Development Areas will repeat or interrupt this pattern.
Key concepts or framework: Environmental racism framework: analyzes how transportation decisions distribute benefits and burdens along racial lines through exclusion from planning, localized burdens, and unequal mobility access. White noose: the ring of suburban opportunity surrounding racially segregated urban cores. Racism without racists: discriminatory outcomes produced by facially neutral technical criteria layered onto an already segregated geography.
Paper Title: Race, Space, and Struggles for Mobility: Transportation Impacts on African Americans in Oakland and the East Bay
Quotable moment: "racism without racists" (p. 24).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports both halves of the claim. It documents historically uneven mobility access rooted in de jure discrimination, and shows that even facially race neutral, seemingly participatory regional planning processes reproduced exclusion because minority communities' participation and race equity concerns hit real limits within MTC's decision making.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper grounds the section's exclusion claim in a landmark case, showing that race neutral transit funding formulas, layered onto a metropolitan geography built by decades of overt discrimination, can reproduce racial exclusion without any single discriminatory actor. It cautions that formally inclusive planning processes do not guarantee equity when minority participation hits structural limits.

Central claim: A scoping review of 26 studies finds implementation science frameworks exist for active and sustainable transportation interventions, but only nine explicitly address equity, and community engagement, partnerships, and funding operate as both facilitators and barriers to equitable implementation.
Gap or limitation: Only 26 of over 8,500 screened studies met inclusion criteria, and most frameworks that do address equity were developed for Western contexts, which the review itself notes may not transfer to other institutional settings such as China.
Key concepts or framework: Implementation science: the study of methods and factors that determine whether evidence-based interventions get adopted in practice. Barriers and facilitators: context-specificity, community engagement and participation, partnerships and collaboration, and funding; the same factors can enable or block equitable implementation depending on how they are handled.
Paper Title: Implementation science frameworks for active and sustainable transportation interventions with a focus on equity: A scoping review
Quotable moment: "excluding some from participating bequeaths unequal powers among stakeholders" (p. 14, McCullogh et al. quoting Al-Sharari, 2022, p. 1316).
Relevance to argument: Supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half, showing that fair representation and participation is necessary for equitable implementation, yet the studies reviewed report groups being actively ignored or deterred by feeling they lack the expertise to engage with complex infrastructure projects, producing unequal power among stakeholders.
Synthesis paragraph: This review shows that even when implementation frameworks name community engagement as a success factor, marginalized groups are frequently excluded or deterred from participating, concentrating power among project proponents rather than affected communities. It supports the section's exclusion claim while cautioning that most equity-focused frameworks are Western in origin and may not travel well to other contexts.

Central claim: Transportation injustice is a product of systemic racism and ableism that compounds for people who are both Black and disabled, since public transit systems were built around an ideal rider who is economically secure, able bodied, and white. Dismantling it requires an intersectional, mobility justice approach centering the leadership of those most impacted.
Gap or limitation: The authors note a dearth of evidence at the intersection of race and disability specifically, since disability studies tend to exclude race and race studies tend to omit disability, leaving this population understudied.
Key concepts or framework: Transportation injustice: structural conditions that perpetuate inequities, discrimination, and exclusion based on disability, race, class, gender, and age. Intersectionality: overlapping social identities compound rather than simply add experiences of discrimination. Crip Mobility Justice: a framework prioritizing accessibility, interdependence, and abolition of policing alongside physical infrastructure.
Paper Title: Inclusive Mobility: Dismantling transportation injustice at the intersection of race and disability
Quotable moment: "The administration did not seek input from the Department of Transportation, Baltimore citizens, or community groups on this decision" (p. 2).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports both halves of the claim. It traces mobility exclusion to slavery, redlining, and highway construction, and gives a concrete contemporary case: Maryland canceling the Black-serving Red Line to fund the whiter Purple Line without seeking input from Baltimore residents or community groups.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper grounds the section's claim in a concrete recent case, Maryland defunding the Black-serving Red Line for the whiter Purple Line without community input, while tracing the same exclusionary pattern back through redlining and highway construction. It argues dismantling this requires sharing decision-making power with Black and disabled communities as leaders, not only building accessible infrastructure.

Central claim: A literature review of transportation equity research finds that horizontal equity, equal treatment of similar groups, and vertical equity, prioritizing disadvantaged populations, remain inconsistently defined and measured across studies, and that clearer frameworks, better data, and more inclusive decision-making are needed to close this gap.
Gap or limitation: The review draws on a single geographic context, and the authors acknowledge that transportation inequities and appropriate remedies vary substantially by density and region, limiting how directly its recommendations transfer.
Key concepts or framework: Horizontal equity: equal treatment of individuals or groups with similar needs. Vertical equity: allocating resources based on differing needs, prioritizing disadvantaged groups. Accessibility indices and affordability metrics: quantitative tools used alongside community engagement approaches to assess whether a transportation system is equitable.
Paper Title: Inclusive and Accessible Transportation for All: Strategies for Integrating Equity in Transportation Research
Quotable moment: "Inclusive decision-making processes that involve underrepresented communities will ensure that their voices are considered" (p. 25).
Relevance to argument: A thinner fit than most sources in this section: this is a broad measurement focused literature review rather than a case study of participation or exclusion. It touches the unevenly distributed half by cataloging accessibility and affordability metrics, and gestures at the participation half only in its closing recommendation for more inclusive, community-driven decision-making.
Synthesis paragraph: This review is useful mainly as a map of how transportation equity gets measured, horizontal versus vertical equity, accessibility indices, affordability metrics, rather than as evidence of participation's role in preventing exclusion. It is included with that caveat: its value here is cataloging the measurement landscape the section's case studies push back against.

Central claim: Interviews and field observations with the San Jose Bike Party, a monthly mass cycling ride organized via social media, find participants hold contested and often depoliticized understandings of the event as collective action, complicating claims that social media organizing democratizes civic participation.
Gap or limitation: The paper does not analyze whether SJBP has produced any actual change in cycling infrastructure, planning, or policy, and the authors explicitly flag this as a needed direction for future research.
Key concepts or framework: Prefigurative politics: enacting the change one advocates for through the form of the collective action itself, here temporarily claiming road space for cyclists. Virtual activism: activism organized through social media platforms, of contested lasting impact. Democratic divide: unequal ability to participate in a movement based on access to its digital organizing platforms.
Paper Title: Is the medium the message? Exploring the intersection of social media and collective action in the San Jose Bike Party
Quotable moment: "the ride route, which is exclusively posted on electronic platforms" (p. 10).
Relevance to argument: A thinner fit for this section's specific claim: the study centers a recreational social movement rather than an infrastructure planning process, and most participants did not describe SJBP as political. Its relevance is indirect, since the authors connect it to broader questions of equity, access, and inclusion in cycling infrastructure advocacy, without empirically testing that connection here.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper is included as a boundary case rather than a direct source: it studies grassroots cycling collective action, not infrastructure planning, and finds participants' political motives were often muddled rather than clear. Its value to the section is the authors' own gesture toward equity focused cycling infrastructure advocacy, a connection this study raises but does not test.

Central claim: Despite civil rights and environmental justice mandates, transportation planning continues to disproportionately burden low income and minority communities because public involvement processes rarely give residents real influence over decisions. The paper proposes a three step model: community led identification of needs, dedicated funding to meet them, and community derived metrics to track progress.
Gap or limitation: The model's case studies are drawn from California, a state with an unusually strong environmental justice advocacy history and well resourced community based organizations, which the authors note may limit transferability elsewhere.
Key concepts or framework: Just process versus just outcomes: meaningful involvement of historically burdened communities versus fair distribution of benefits and burdens. Priority unmet needs: a model of equity grounded in what communities themselves identify as needed, not abstract quantitative equity analysis. Participatory budgeting: dedicating funds directly to needs identified through community deliberation.
Paper Title: Achieving transportation equity: Meaningful public involvement to meet the needs of underserved communities
Quotable moment: "a near-absence of meaningful public involvement through which affected residents can influence and shape decisions" (p. 2 of the author preprint).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. It argues traditional public involvement is a near absence of meaningful engagement, and proposes a concrete alternative in which community identified needs receive dedicated funding, directly linking genuine participation to just infrastructure outcomes rather than treating them as separate.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper offers the section's participatory alternative in concrete, actionable form: community identified needs tied to dedicated funding and community derived metrics, rather than public involvement as a box checking exercise. It reinforces that meaningful participation and just outcomes are not separable goals, directly grounding the exclusion half of the claim in an implementable model.

Central claim: Case studies of Amsterdam's North-South Metro line and Sydney's Parramatta Rail Link find that technical, model driven transport planning consistently overlooks social impacts, contributing to lost social licence, poor communication, and inadequate protection of affected communities. Social Impact Assessment, applied early, offers a path to better integrate social issues into megaproject planning.
Gap or limitation: The study examines only two rail megaprojects in wealthy, high capacity planning contexts, Amsterdam and Sydney, so it may understate the barriers to adopting Social Impact Assessment in lower resourced planning systems.
Key concepts or framework: Social Impact Assessment: a framework for anticipating and managing how projects change people's lives, distinct from purely economic or engineering impact models. Social licence to operate: a community's ongoing acceptance of a project, lost through poor communication and unmet commitments. Predict and provide: a quantitative, model driven planning approach criticized for ignoring wider social context.
Paper Title: Limitations of Technical Approaches to Transport Planning Practice in Two Cases: Social Issues as a Critical Component of Urban Projects
Quotable moment: "dilute the capacity of the public to contribute meaningfully to transport planning" (p. 15).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. Both rail megaprojects show that public consultation occurring late in the project lifecycle fails to transfer community input into how social impacts get assessed and managed, diluting the public's capacity to meaningfully shape infrastructure that affects them.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper shows, through two concrete megaproject cases, that consultation without a mechanism to feed into actual project design amounts to participation in name only. It reinforces the exclusion claim by tracing the same failure, technical dominance sidelining community input, across two different high income cities, and proposes Social Impact Assessment as a structural fix rather than a procedural add on.

Central claim: Focus groups with mobility disabled people and low income women in Berlin's Graefekiez neighborhood find that non-participation in street space reallocation planning stems from feeling excluded and ignored by prior participatory processes, while a purpose built, transdisciplinary research format better reflected residents' lived expertise.
Gap or limitation: The case study is a single Berlin neighborhood under a specific green party led local government, and the authors note it is not perfectly generalizable to other transport planning contexts.
Key concepts or framework: Lived expertise: the practical, embodied knowledge structurally disadvantaged people hold about their own mobility needs, distinct from technical planning expertise. Invited versus claimed spaces: participation opportunities designed by authorities versus spaces residents create themselves. Negative political self-efficacy: the learned sense that speaking up in official participatory venues will not lead anywhere.
Paper Title: Lived expertise of the structurally disadvantaged: towards a more just participatory transport planning process
Quotable moment: "I've been talking to and against walls for years" (p. 11).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. It shows concretely how invited participatory spaces, meant to democratize a car space reallocation project, actively discouraged the structurally disadvantaged residents they claimed to include, reproducing the same exclusion the project intended to fix.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper offers a vivid, first person account of how official participation processes can actively produce the disengagement they are meant to prevent, directly reinforcing the claim that infrastructure decisions without genuine participation reproduce exclusion. It also models an alternative, a co-designed research format residents experienced as more welcoming and reflective of their lived expertise.

Central claim: Interviews with 23 urban development professionals across U.S. cities find a shift toward more explicitly equitable practices, driven less by government initiative than by community-based organizations and residents adopting radical demands for redistributed resources, alongside strategic framing to counter opposition rooted in individualist and racialized cultural mindsets.
Gap or limitation: The study relies on 23 interviews with professionals rather than the residents whose neighborhoods are affected, and the authors note a remaining knowledge gap about the cultural mindsets that drive opposition to equitable development in particular places.
Key concepts or framework: Bottom-up transformation: resident and CBO led initiatives that go beyond procedural inclusion to shift actual resource distribution and power. Bootstraps narrative: a cultural myth of unconstrained individual mobility used to oppose equitable investment. Tactical urbanism: temporary, small scale interventions, such as youth-led road redesigns, used to demonstrate what permanent infrastructure change could look like.
Paper Title: Mindsets and actions: Shifts in equitable and sustainable development in U.S. cities
Quotable moment: "this would not have happened" without the youth-led project, which "sort of elevated it for [the state agency]" and "showed what was possible" (p. 11).
Relevance to argument: A moderate fit: transportation is one of several urban development domains covered alongside housing and parks, not the primary focus. Where most relevant, a youth-led tactical urbanism project redesigning a high-fatality road, it shows infrastructure change becoming possible only after community-led action pushed a reluctant state agency, illustrating the participation half concretely though not exclusively about mobility.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper is useful mainly for its broader pattern, that community-led pressure, not government initiative, has been the main driver of recent shifts toward equitable urban development, with a concrete mobility example, youth redesigning a dangerous road, illustrating how bottom-up organizing can force infrastructure change agencies would not have pursued alone.

Central claim: A literature review of global best practices finds that technology driven mobility solutions, such as MaaS platforms and accessible transit systems, improve equity for vulnerable groups only when paired with inclusive land use planning, affordable design, and active community participation, and that rural regions and non-elderly vulnerable groups remain understudied.
Gap or limitation: The reviewed literature is itself urban centric with limited rural evidence and no longitudinal data, and the paper is a review of secondary sources rather than original fieldwork with vulnerable communities.
Journal or Proceedings: TeMA - Journal of Land Use, Mobility and Environment, 18(1), 95-112
Key concepts or framework: Mobility-as-a-Service: a digital platform integrating multiple transport modes into one accessible interface. Intersectional mobility vulnerability: overlapping identities such as gender, disability, race, and economic status that compound transportation barriers. Digital divide: unequal access to the devices and connectivity that ICT-based mobility solutions assume users already have.
Paper Title: Mobilising equity. Emerging evidence for integrating vulnerable communities
Quotable moment: "engagement must go beyond consultation, requiring active citizen participation in planning" (p. 15).
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half by cataloging how rural regions and multiple vulnerable groups remain underserved despite smart mobility advancements. It touches the participation half more lightly, noting that engagement must go beyond consultation to active participation in planning, without providing its own case study of that shift.
Synthesis paragraph: This review is most useful for documenting the uneven distribution half, showing that smart mobility technologies leave rural residents and several vulnerable groups behind despite their promise. Its treatment of participation is brief and aspirational rather than evidenced, so it complements rather than substitutes for the section's more direct participatory case studies.

Central claim: Drawing on research into unhoused, disabled, and aging city dwellers, this book argues that mobility injustice is produced by everyday design choices, benches angled to prevent sleeping, high curbs, short pedestrian crossing signals, not only by policy, and asks who the built world is actually designed for.
