Gap or limitation: Only the introduction and bibliography were available in the extracted preview; the book's empirical chapters on unhoused, disabled, and aging populations, where the fieldwork evidence lives, could not be reviewed here and should be read directly for case level detail.
Key concepts or framework: Exclusionary design: material and spatial choices, intentional or not, that curb the mobility of vulnerable groups. Mobility justice: a framework asking who has the right to move, treating autonomous mobility as a fiction sustained by hidden assistance and dependency. Design justice: extending questions of justice to the artifacts and spaces that afford or restrict movement.
Paper Title: Mobility Injustice by Design
Quotable moment: "Who is the built world built for?" (p. 15, Jensen quoting Hendren, 2020).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half, reframing exclusion as encoded in physical design decisions, hostile benches, curbs, crossing timers, rather than only in planning process or funding. This entry draws only on the book's introductory chapter and bibliography, since the empirical fieldwork chapters were not included in the available preview text.
Synthesis paragraph: This book pushes the section's exclusion claim down to the level of material design, arguing that hostile benches, high curbs, and short crossing signals encode exclusion into infrastructure independent of any single planning decision. Only the introductory framing was available here; the book's later chapters presumably supply fieldwork evidence for unhoused, disabled, and aging Copenhageners that would let this claim be checked against lived experience.

Central claim: A focus group of 16 public transport and disability advocacy practitioners in Victoria, Australia finds that Melbourne's privatized, splintered transport network creates cognitive access barriers for people with intellectual disability that no single service provider can fix alone, requiring network wide collaboration and inclusive participation mechanisms.
Gap or limitation: The study draws on a single one day focus group of practitioners and advocates rather than people with intellectual disability directly, and is limited to one metropolitan transport system in Victoria, Australia.
Key concepts or framework: Mobility justice: understanding mobility outcomes as generated at the intersection of transport systems and wider social circumstances, here extended to cognitive access. Splintered urbanism: fragmented, privatized transport governance in which competing operators communicate inconsistently. Performative research: a focus group method aimed at prompting collaboration and change, not just recording existing conditions.
Paper Title: Mobility justice and accessible public transport networks for people with intellectual disability
Quotable moment: "too often, people with disability are not paid for their expertise" (p. 13).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half. It shows existing participatory mechanisms, access committees and reference groups, systematically underrepresent people with intellectual disability, and argues genuine inclusion requires network wide collaboration across privatized operators plus fair compensation for advocates' expertise.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper extends the participation half of the claim to an overlooked group, showing that even disability focused participatory structures in transport planning routinely exclude people with intellectual disability, and that meaningful inclusion requires paid, coordinated, network wide effort rather than one-off consultation. It grounds the claim in a concrete account of how existing inclusion mechanisms quietly reproduce exclusion.

Central claim: Interviews with 13 city planners, transportation employees, and state representatives in North Florida find that funding shortfalls and misaligned priorities among stakeholders, not lack of awareness, are the main barriers to equitable transportation for mobility vulnerable populations, and that new technologies are being piloted without yet translating into improved access for those groups.
Gap or limitation: The study interviewed only 13 stakeholders, all transportation professionals, and the authors note responses may be shaped by participants' professional roles or concern about their employers rather than by mobility vulnerable residents' own perspectives.
Key concepts or framework: Mobility vulnerable populations: residents below the poverty line, people with disabilities, and older adults with limited transportation options. SWOT framework: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats used to structure stakeholders' assessment of the transportation system. Smart Cities Collaborative: a multi city initiative piloting technologies like autonomous rideshare intended to reduce transportation disparities.
Paper Title: North Florida Stakeholder Perspectives: Gaps, Barriers, and Facilitators in the Transportation System
Quotable moment: "Politicians come and go. They have priorities, and they do not always match [the priorities of multiple stakeholders]" (p. 7).
Relevance to argument: A moderate fit for the unevenly distributed half, since it documents professionals' own acknowledgment that funding and priorities are misaligned with mobility vulnerable and minority populations. It is thinner on the participation half: the study centers professional perspectives rather than community members, and stakeholders admit new technologies have not yet been communicated to the users they are meant to serve.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper documents uneven distribution from the professional side, showing transportation officials themselves recognize that funding and political priorities leave some communities, especially higher minority areas, underserved. It is a weaker source for the participation half, since it centers professionals' self-assessment rather than mobility vulnerable residents' direct accounts of exclusion.

Central claim: Survey data from 664 Ningbo, China residents show social participation, not physical infrastructure or technology acceptance, is the strongest predictor of older adults' unmet travel demand, while health barriers and functional capacity constrain trips differently for middle aged and 75-plus age groups respectively.
Gap or limitation: Only the abstract, highlights, and introduction of this paywalled article were accessible for this review; the methods, results tables, and discussion sections could not be verified against the source text and should be checked directly before citing specific findings.
Journal or Proceedings: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice, 211, 105130
Key concepts or framework: Latent travel demand: unmet mobility need operationalized across four dimensions, health barriers, functional capacity, social participation, and technology acceptance. Active aging: a WHO framework treating older adults as active social participants rather than passive recipients of protection.
Paper Title: Quantification of latent travel demand across age groups with a focus on older adults: a theoretical framework with empirical evidence from China
Quotable moment: "age-friendly policy should move beyond physical infrastructure improvement alone" (p. 2, Abstract).
Relevance to argument: A thinner fit for this section: the paper documents unmet travel demand among an aging population through quantitative modeling rather than a case of infrastructure built without community participation. It is included as background evidence that equity in older adult mobility may hinge on social participation opportunities rather than only accessible infrastructure.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper is a thin, quantitative complement to the section's argument: it shows that even for older adults, a group facing well documented mobility barriers, unmet travel demand is driven more by social participation opportunities than infrastructure alone. Only the paper's abstract and introduction were available for this review.

Central claim: A four month federal funding suspension halted a community engaged research project meant to center environmental justice organizations in California climate and transportation planning, illustrating how federal science funding disruptions directly reduce vulnerable communities' opportunities to shape infrastructure and climate decisions.
Gap or limitation: As a first person perspective piece about the authors' own disrupted project, it reports process and consequences rather than completed empirical findings on community risk perceptions, since the underlying data collection itself was interrupted.
Key concepts or framework: Epistemic justice: valuing community knowledge as a legitimate form of data on par with quantitative measures. Techno-rational planning: transportation planning dominated by quantitative metrics that can miss lived safety and health concerns communities identify directly. Community-informed data tools: indices like CalEnviroScreen that incorporate community perspectives into official risk assessments.
Paper Title: Beyond research delays: science funding disruptions limit community participation in climate and infrastructure planning
Quotable moment: "the street lacks lighting to illuminate the path at night" (p. 2).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half, but through a distinct mechanism: federal funding cuts, not just planning process design, can abruptly cut off the pipeline that lets community knowledge enter climate and transportation decision making, disproportionately affecting the vulnerable communities the project was meant to serve.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper adds a distinct mechanism to the exclusion claim: federal funding volatility itself can sever the pipeline connecting community knowledge to infrastructure and climate planning, not just weak local process design. It shows concretely how techno-rational transportation metrics miss lived safety concerns communities can name directly, reinforcing why participation must be actively resourced rather than assumed to continue.

Central claim: Reviewing environmental justice and public involvement literature, the authors argue transportation agencies have focused on distributional justice, who bears costs and benefits, while under-theorizing procedural justice, and propose four process metrics plus Structured Public Involvement as a large-group method to make public involvement more inclusive and measurable.
Gap or limitation: The paper is a conference proceedings submission rather than a peer-reviewed journal article, and its proposed Structured Public Involvement approach is illustrated mainly through the authors' own prior projects rather than independent replication.
Key concepts or framework: Distributional versus procedural justice: the Rawlsian distinction between fair outcomes and fair decision-making processes, the latter chronically under-researched in transportation EJ work. Arnstein Ladder: a scale of public involvement levels used to benchmark how much power a process gives participants. Q-metric: a stakeholder-reported measure of process satisfaction used to evaluate Structured Public Involvement events.
Paper Title: Towards Environmental Justice in Transportation Decision Making using Structured Public Involvement
Quotable moment: "asked the citizens to return to their respective interest organizations and identify only one or two persons" (p. 16).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half with a documented example: a Virginia DOT advisory committee that shrank from 70 interested citizens to about 30 hand-picked representatives, held up in agency literature as a model process despite excluding most of the public who showed up.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper's VDOT example is a vivid, documented instance of the exclusion the section describes: an agency-praised process that literally turned away most of the public who showed up to keep the group small. It reinforces that procedural justice, not just distributional outcomes, needs its own metrics, since existing EJ practice has focused far more on who bears costs than on whether decision processes are genuinely inclusive.

Central claim: Twenty six interviews with people with diverse visible and invisible disabilities in an Australian city find that dignified mobility depends on accessible infrastructure, inclusive information, and respectful staff interactions across an entire journey, and that a single inaccessible link anywhere in that journey makes participants vulnerable to indignity.
Gap or limitation: The study is limited to bus and train systems in one Australian city and does not examine taxis, light rail, ferries, or air travel, or factors like time of day and trip purpose.
Key concepts or framework: Dignified mobility experience: a dynamic interaction between personal preferences, impairment specific needs, infrastructure, staff interactions, and information accessibility across a full journey. Compliance based accessibility: standards like the ADA or Australia's Disability Standards for Accessible Public Transport that rely on voluntary or partial compliance, so meeting a broad standard can still exclude people whose needs it did not anticipate.
Paper Title: The dignity experience of people with disability when using trains and buses in an Australian city
Quotable moment: "being treated like everyone else" (p. 8).
Relevance to argument: Supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half by showing that standards developed without embedding diverse disabled people's specific needs in planning can be formally met while still excluding them, and argues policy mandates for including people with diverse impairments in planning are urgently needed.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper treats dignity, not just physical access, as the measure of whether transport infrastructure includes disabled people, and traces failures back to compliance based standards built without disabled people's specific needs embedded in planning. It reinforces that infrastructure designed without participation reproduces exclusion, even when it technically satisfies accessibility law.

Central claim: A conceptual literature review argues that AV deployment's environmental sustainability gains and social equity impacts are deeply intertwined rather than separate concerns, and proposes an integrated framework built on proactive planning, meaningful community engagement, and adaptive governance to keep AV deployment from disproportionately burdening marginalized communities.
Gap or limitation: Only the abstract, highlights, introduction, and truncated section previews of this paywalled article were accessible; the full literature review, framework details, and discussion could not be read and should be verified directly before citing specific claims from those sections.
Key concepts or framework: Equity-environmental sustainability nexus: the claim that AV emissions benefits and social equity outcomes are interdependent, so optimizing one without the other risks negative net outcomes. Siloed AV research: the paper's diagnosis that policy, planning, and assessment frameworks currently treat equity and sustainability separately. Social equity: fair distribution of benefits and burdens ensuring equal access regardless of socioeconomic status.
Paper Title: The equity-environmental sustainability nexus in autonomous vehicles: An integrated framework for policy and planning
Quotable moment: "ensuring AVs contribute positively to a future that is both green and fair" (p. 2, Abstract).
Relevance to argument: A moderate, AV specific fit for the section: it names meaningful community engagement as a required component of just AV deployment, directly echoing the participation half of the claim, though at the level of a conceptual framework proposal rather than an empirical case. Most useful for feeding the broader Mobility as Social Service argument given its direct AV focus.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper's main relevance is naming meaningful community engagement as a required element of just AV deployment, directly connecting to the section's participation claim within the AV context central to the broader project. Because only the introduction and truncated section previews were accessible, its literature review and framework specifics should be verified from the full text before being cited in detail.

Central claim: Qualitative interviews in Toronto's Rexdale neighborhood find that repeated experiences of transport poverty, including racism and harassment on transit, shape marginalized residents' travel attitudes and behavior beyond material deprivation alone, and that delayed transit infrastructure investment compounds this by leaving equity-deserving communities without the reliable service needed to sustain positive attitudes toward transit.
Gap or limitation: The qualitative, cross-sectional study covers a single marginalized population in one Toronto neighborhood, and the authors call for testing the framework quantitatively and in other populations and geographies.
Key concepts or framework: Transport poverty: the combined effect of social and transportation disadvantages that limit mobility. Perceived behavioural control: a person's sense of their own capacity to choose a travel mode, shaped by past experience of poverty and discrimination. Affective versus cognitive attitude: emotional responses to unsafe or discriminatory transit experiences that drive behavior more than favorable abstract opinions about transit.
Paper Title: Travelling in the margins: Impacts of transport poverty on travel attitudes and behaviours
Quotable moment: "transportation should be considered as a social policy issue in and beyond Toronto" (p. 15).
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half directly through Rexdale residents' lived experience of transport poverty, and touches the participation half by naming repeated, undelivered infrastructure promises, the delayed Finch West LRT and the closed Line 3 subway serving Scarborough, as a pattern of underinvestment in equity-deserving neighborhoods that compounds distrust.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper extends the uneven distribution claim into the psychological register, showing that transport poverty shapes not just access but attitudes and trust toward transit, and that repeated delays to infrastructure meant for equity deserving neighborhoods reinforce that distrust. It supports treating transportation as a social policy issue rather than a purely technical one.

Central claim: A national survey and interviews with Canadian local elected officials find they have little direct experience with transportation barriers like unaffordability, disability, or harassment, and while they broadly support procedural equity, they are divided on prioritizing marginalized communities in transportation investment, revealing a disconnect from academic and professional equity discourse.
Gap or limitation: The study surveys elected officials' self-reported values and experience rather than observing actual investment decisions or outcomes, and non-response bias may mean officials less interested in equity were underrepresented.
Key concepts or framework: Procedural equity: fair decision-making process, distinguished from substantive equity, which prioritizes marginalized communities in resource allocation. Technical-rational model: the tendency of transportation research to treat politicians as external to decision-making rather than examining their own values and political context. Fundamental mismatch: a gap between who makes transit decisions and who is most affected by them.
Paper Title: Transportation barriers and equity: Values and experiences of elected officials
Quotable moment: "a fundamental mismatch between who is making key transit decisions . . . and who is most affected by those decisions" (p. 2, Linovski et al. quoting TransitCenter, 2022, p. 5).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half by locating the disconnect at the level of who holds decision-making power in the first place. It shows that the people making transportation investment decisions are demographically and experientially unlike the marginalized communities those decisions most affect.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper locates the exclusion the section describes at its source, showing that the officials who control transportation investment decisions rarely share the lived experience of transportation barriers themselves, and are divided on whether to prioritize marginalized communities even while endorsing fair process. It reframes participation not just as who gets consulted but as who governs.

Central claim: Using 2017 National Household Travel Survey data and a logit model, this study finds that unmet travel needs among people with disabilities vary sharply by race, gender, poverty, and age, and that Hispanic PWD and disabled stay-at-home mothers report suppressed rather than absent travel needs due to systemic barriers and reliance on community trust over formal services.
Gap or limitation: The analysis relies on a single cross-sectional national survey and infers suppressed need indirectly from reduced travel patterns rather than through direct qualitative accounts of why travel was curtailed.
Journal or Proceedings: International Journal of Transportation Science and Technology
Key concepts or framework: Unfulfilled travel need: reduced travel that reflects suppressed aspirations under systemic barriers rather than satisfied mobility. Intersectionality: overlapping identities, disability, race, gender, poverty, that compound and complicate travel disadvantage in ways single-category analysis misses. Suppressed mobility: travel demand that goes unreported because barriers have taught people not to expect service.
Paper Title: Investigating unfulfilled travel needs for people with travel-limiting conditions using the 2017 National Household Travel Survey (NHTS) data
Quotable moment: "a constrained ability to fulfill their desired travel needs" (p. 14).
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half with quantitative evidence that disability intersects with race, gender, and poverty to produce distinct patterns of suppressed travel need, arguing that transportation equity requires proactive, culturally competent outreach rather than only responding to demand that is already expressed.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper adds a methodological caution to the unevenly distributed claim: measured travel frequency can hide suppressed need, especially for groups like Hispanic PWD who trust community networks over formal transportation services after learning not to expect accommodation. It argues equity requires actively uncovering suppressed demand, not just responding to requests already made.

Central claim: Reviewing U.S. transportation policy and mobility justice theory, this paper argues Universal Basic Mobility should combine three elements, treating mobility as essential to well-being, targeting resources toward those facing transportation insecurity, and pairing subsidy with adequate service, to avoid repeating past piecemeal, single-mode policies that failed to reduce poverty.
Gap or limitation: The paper is a conceptual policy review rather than an empirical evaluation of any specific UBM pilot program, so its three-part framework has not yet been tested against outcomes data.
Key concepts or framework: Mobility justice: an expanded understanding of mobility as freedom of movement and capability, not just travel speed, central to societal participation and power. Targeted universalism: providing resources unevenly, prioritizing those experiencing transportation insecurity, rather than distributing identical resources to everyone. Transportation insecurity: inability to move safely or in a timely way, concentrated among low income, non-White, and disabled populations.
Paper Title: The promise of Universal Basic Mobility
Quotable moment: "mobility resources are unevenly distributed, so the state must target such resources" (p. 14).
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half by tracing transportation insecurity to historical disparities in car access along race and income lines, and connects to the participation half by arguing mobility justice requires centering the voices of those experiencing transportation disparities rather than designing policy around a single mode.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper offers the section a policy level articulation of both claim halves: transportation insecurity is unevenly distributed along race and income lines rooted in decades of car access disparities, and mobility justice requires centering the voices of those most affected rather than designing policy around a single mode. It positions Universal Basic Mobility as a concrete framework for practice.

Central claim: A narrative review of built environment and subjective well-being research since 2021 finds that public transport investment supports well-being and reduces social exclusion, but can also trigger transit-led gentrification and displacement of economically vulnerable residents, while private car access benefits individual users at the cost of collective health and equity externalities.
Gap or limitation: As a narrative rather than systematic review, study selection relied on the author's framework and judgment, may exclude relevant studies with a less obvious fit, and draws mainly on English-language research underrepresenting the Global South.
Key concepts or framework: Pathways framework: a conceptual model linking built environment attributes to subjective well-being through life domains like accessibility, work, and social relationships. Transit-led gentrification: new public transport investment attracting more affluent residents and raising housing costs, eroding accessibility benefits meant for existing lower income residents. Mobility-related exclusion: reduced social participation and well-being for those without car access in car-oriented environments.
Paper Title: Urban planning, the built environment, and subjective well-being: A review of recent research advances
Quotable moment: "Planning processes could include participatory approaches which enable the representation of diverse voices" (p. 12).
Relevance to argument: A broad, thinner fit for this section: transportation is one of five review categories in a wide-ranging well-being literature synthesis rather than a dedicated case study. It is most useful for the unevenly distributed half, documenting transit-led displacement and mobility exclusion for non-drivers, and briefly names participatory planning as a needed but underused equity tool.
Synthesis paragraph: This review's main relevance is documenting that even beneficial transit investments can produce uneven well-being outcomes through displacement, and that the literature calls for participatory planning to represent diverse voices in built environment decisions. As a broad synthesis spanning far beyond transportation, it functions as supporting context rather than a dedicated case for this section's participation claim.

Central claim: A multidimensional framework combining household housing and transportation cost burden with individual level health, safety, comfort, accessibility, and time constraints finds that low income households in car dependent central Texas suppress travel demand, and that Black and Hispanic single mother households experience disproportionately severe intra-personal travel constraints.
Gap or limitation: Only the abstract, highlights, and introduction of this paywalled article were accessible; the full methodology, results tables, and discussion could not be read and should be verified directly before citing specific quantitative findings.
Key concepts or framework: Housing and Transportation Cost-to-Income Ratio: a household level affordability measure combining housing and travel costs against income. Intra-personal Travel Constraints propensity: an individual level model estimating the probability of facing health, safety, comfort, accessibility, or time barriers to reaching desired destinations. Suppressed travel demand: reduced travel driven by constraint rather than preference.
Paper Title: Who faces travel constraints? Analyzing household and individual travel challenges in automobile-dependent central Texas
Quotable moment: "single-mother households displayed distinct patterns of constraint" (p. 2, Abstract).
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half with a granular, intersectional account of who bears travel constraints in an automobile dependent region, showing race and gender compound to concentrate the most severe constraints among Black and Hispanic single mothers, and that expanding non-automobile options is necessary to address it.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper adds fine-grained, intersectional evidence to the uneven distribution claim, showing that in a car dependent region, travel constraints concentrate most severely among Black and Hispanic single mother households once both affordability and personal barriers are measured together. Only the paper's abstract and introduction were available for this review.

Central claim: The authors argue transportation planning should shift from state-centered equity analyses, which mostly measure and reform how benefits and burdens are distributed, toward transportation justice, which demands structural redistribution of political power and resources and treats residents' active participation in decisions as essential, drawing on hybrid case studies where community organizing reshaped state planning outcomes.
Gap or limitation: The hybrid case studies described are exceptional, well-organized regional coalitions capable of contending with state agencies on their own terms, so the paper's own examples suggest this level of organizing capacity may not be replicable everywhere.
Key concepts or framework: Transportation equity versus transportation justice: equity as reform of distribution within existing state processes, justice as transformation of the structures and power relations producing inequity. Pro forma public involvement: participation processes solicited to satisfy legal requirements that are unlikely to affect final decisions. Hybrid state and society-centric strategies: community organizations using state planning processes and technical analyses to win real concessions.
Paper Title: From transportation equity to transportation justice: Within, through, and beyond the state
Quotable moment: "it is often pro forma, and its results are unlikely to affect ultimate decisions" (p. 3 of the author manuscript).
Relevance to argument: Directly and centrally supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half, and gives concrete counter-examples of genuine participation's effect: a Fresno community-led needs assessment that exposed how little transit access reached identified disadvantaged communities and won a dedicated grant program, and a Bay Area community-developed equity scenario that outperformed the regional agency's preferred plan and won funding concessions.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper offers the section's clearest theoretical statement of the exclusion claim, distinguishing equity as reform from justice as transformation of power, and backs it with two concrete wins, Fresno's community-led needs assessment and the Bay Area's community-authored equity scenario, where organized participation changed what got funded and built. It also cautions that such wins required unusually well-organized coalitions.

Central claim: Using a Maximal Covering Location Problem model applied to Hilliard, Ohio, this study finds that adding roughly 26 to 36 new bus stops chosen through spatial optimization can increase transit access coverage for origin- and destination-based transport disadvantaged areas by around 70 to 78 percent.
Gap or limitation: The model treats equity solely as spatial coverage and demand estimated from data, with no field validation of whether the transport disadvantaged residents identified would actually use or want the proposed new stops.
Journal or Proceedings: International Journal of Geospatial and Environmental Research, 7(1), Article 2
Key concepts or framework: Transport disadvantaged: people who need public transportation because they lack access to personal vehicles, often left unserved by transit built around able bodied commuters. Maximal Covering Location Problem: an optimization model that selects facility locations to maximize coverage of a defined demand. Bi-objective model: weighting origin-based and destination-based demand together to find stop locations serving both simultaneously.
Paper Title: Enhancing Equity in Public Transportation Using Geographic Information Systems and Spatial Optimization
Quotable moment: "some people are excluded from the right of mobility and accessibility" (p. 3).
Relevance to argument: A thin fit for this section: the paper is a purely technical GIS optimization study demonstrating how facility placement can mathematically improve coverage for transport disadvantaged areas, but it does not address community participation in decisions at all, illustrating the kind of top-down, technically-defined equity analysis the section's argument pushes against.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper exemplifies the technical, top-down equity analysis the section contrasts with participatory approaches: it optimizes bus stop locations mathematically to improve coverage for transport disadvantaged areas without any described role for affected residents in defining need or reviewing outcomes. It is useful as a contrast case showing what equity work looks like when treated as a spatial optimization problem alone.

Central claim: A systematic review of academic papers, agency reports, and TRB conference materials finds that equity remains inconsistently integrated into transportation scenario planning, especially for newer scenarios involving emerging technology, and recommends embedding vertical equity analysis and advanced community participation techniques throughout all four phases of the scenario planning process.
Gap or limitation: As a review of existing literature and conference materials, the paper's policy recommendations are not yet tested through implementation, and the reviewed practices themselves varied widely in rigor and are unevenly documented.
Key concepts or framework: Vertical equity: allocating costs and benefits based on differing mobility needs, income, and structural inequalities, distinct from horizontal equity's equal treatment of similar groups. Scenario planning: a multi-step process generating and evaluating multiple possible transportation futures rather than one forecast. Community participation as justice-building: training community members in the planning process itself so input can shape long-term plans, not just react to them.
Paper Title: Integrating equity in transportation scenario planning: A systematic review
Quotable moment: "how their participation can affect long-term plans" (p. 21).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half, citing Karner et al.'s point that community participation in scenario planning must go beyond collecting opinions to teaching communities how the process itself works, so their input can actually shape long-term plans rather than being collected and set aside.
Synthesis paragraph: This review reinforces the exclusion claim by showing equity, especially community participation, remains inconsistently built into transportation scenario planning, with newer technology-focused scenarios like electric vehicles particularly likely to skip equity analysis. It draws on Karner et al.'s argument that real participation requires teaching communities the planning process itself, not just soliciting opinions.

Central claim: A policy inventory across 29 African countries and a South African household survey case study find that most transport policies omit or only superficially address people with disabilities, and that South Africans with disabilities take 27 to 66 percent fewer weekly trips than non-disabled residents, evidence of social isolation produced by policy neglect.
Gap or limitation: The authors explicitly state they did not investigate the actual role of community leaders, NGOs, and lobby groups in African transport planning, and recommend this as a direction for future research rather than something this study demonstrates.
Key concepts or framework: Universal design: designing environments to be usable by the greatest range of people, contrasted with policies that address disability only superficially. Transport justice framework: an approach linking space and mobility to accessibility that the authors note tends to overlook how differently embodied people interact with infrastructure. Trip frequency as isolation measure: using reduced trip-making as a quantitative proxy for social exclusion.
Paper Title: Inclusive planning: African policy inventory and South African mobility case study on the exclusion of persons with disabilities
Quotable moment: "people with disability live less integrated, more isolated lives" (p. 10).
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half with cross-national policy evidence and South African trip-rate data showing severe disability related mobility gaps. On participation, the paper recommends including community leaders, NGOs, and disability advocacy groups in ongoing infrastructure projects but explicitly acknowledges it did not investigate their actual role, leaving this a recommendation rather than documented evidence.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper documents severe, quantified disability-related mobility gaps across Africa rooted in policy neglect rather than only infrastructure, supporting the uneven distribution half with concrete trip-rate evidence. Its own honesty about not yet studying community leaders' and disability advocates' actual role in planning marks where the participation half still needs direct empirical grounding.

Central claim: Interviews with transit officials across six Ontario transit authorities find that pandemic-driven service cuts disproportionately harmed low-income and marginalized riders, and that officials, aware of transit equity concerns, had little practical ability to consult transit users before making rapid cuts, most starkly in Windsor's unilateral shutdown of all transit service.
Gap or limitation: The paper centers transit officials' own accounts of their decision-making rather than interviews with the low-income and marginalized riders who bore the impact of service cuts directly.
Key concepts or framework: Transit equity: ensuring public transit service changes do not disproportionately burden those who depend on transit most. Emergency decision-making: rapid, top-down authority, such as a mayor's Emergency Measures Bylaw, that bypasses normal consultation processes during a crisis. Transit poverty: a state in which loss of affordable transit forces reliance on far more expensive alternatives like taxis.
Paper Title: Transit Equity in the Face of the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Study of Six Ontario Transit Authorities
Quotable moment: "Transit groups and users were not consulted prior to this decision being taken" (p. 18).
Relevance to argument: Directly supports the infrastructure without participation reproduces exclusion half with a stark example: a mayor's unilateral, unconsulted decision to shut down an entire transit system, using emergency powers, left thousands without transportation and sparked public opposition, even though officials elsewhere in the study expressed awareness of and concern for transit equity.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper gives the section a sharp, real-time example of the exclusion claim: a mayor's unilateral, unconsulted shutdown of an entire transit system left thousands without transportation, even as officials elsewhere expressed genuine concern for transit equity. It shows that good intentions among decision-makers do not substitute for actual consultation when speed overrides participation.

Central claim: Survey analysis in Baltimore finds people of color, women, low-income, less-educated, and unemployed residents are underrepresented in Baltimore Bike Share membership, with race and gender specifically associated with distinct barriers, safety concerns for women and difficulty riding with children or cargo for nonwhite residents, that uniform system design does not address.
Gap or limitation: The non-user survey has a small sample size that limited the ability to detect effects for some demographic subgroups, and nonresponse bias likely underrepresents residents without regular email access or who are not native English speakers.
Key concepts or framework: Vertical equity: the fair distribution of costs and benefits among groups differing by income or social class, applied here to bike share access. Equity of opportunity versus equity of outcome: whether adequate access has been provided versus whether usage rates actually reflect community demographics. Bike share barriers: safety, personal hygiene, harassment risk, and cargo or child-carrying needs that vary systematically by race and gender.
Paper Title: Bike Share Equity for Underrepresented Groups: Analyzing Barriers to System Usage in Baltimore, Maryland
Quotable moment: "one of the biggest barriers to biking, across all demographic categories, is concern about personal safety" (p. 12).
Relevance to argument: Supports the unevenly distributed half by quantifying who is left out of a specific mobility system and why, and touches the participation half through its policy recommendation for grassroots community outreach, ambassador programs, and community-based design input to reach underrepresented groups rather than relying on system design alone.
Synthesis paragraph: This paper shows that even a supposedly universal mobility service like bike share reproduces exclusion when designed around a narrow user profile, and that closing the gap requires more than infrastructure alone, community outreach and ambassador programs targeted at underrepresented groups. It supports the uneven distribution half with quantified racial and gender specific barriers.

Author(s): Baumann, K., Caldwell, B., Bar, F., & Stokes, B.
Central claim: This paper argues that speculative urban technologies (including self-driving cars) should be co-designed with residents through long-term community storytelling, because doing so builds a community's lasting capacity to shape its own technological future rather than having that future imposed on it.
Gap or limitation: As a one-page extended abstract, it gives little detail on the analysis method or on whether the workshops produced any lasting change for the neighborhood, so it can't fully evidence the durability it claims.
Journal or Proceedings: Extended Abstracts of the 2018 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
Key concepts or framework:
Participatory design fiction: combining real community participation with fictional/speculative technology concepts, so residents react to and reshape a not-yet-real tech.
Infrastructures of the imagination: the idea that a community's ability to picture and steer its own future is something you can deliberately build up, like infrastructure.
Community storytelling: residents author their own scenarios about future tech, instead of researchers authoring them on their behalf.
Paper Title: Community storytelling for speculative urban technologies.
Quotable moment: "By grounding speculative designs in a community context, students and residents imagined novel technologies" (Abstract)
Relevance to argument: This is one of the closest existing precedents for exactly what we did - residents used workshops and a speculative self-driving car concept to shape technology on their own terms, in a community under outside pressure. It directly supports our thread by showing that a speculative AV provocation run through community workshops is a proven way to surface what a community values, which is the core of our "arrives without their participation" critique.
Synthesis paragraph: The literature makes a strong case that workshops paired with a speculative provocation were the right way to surface community values around AVs, a technology that isn't here yet. You can't interview people about something they've never used, and Liao and Muller show why: when a technology isn't part of everyday life, a fictional version is what draws values out. Wong, Omori and Lim, and Sörries prove the mechanism works; a believable speculative artifact gets people treating it as real and voicing values a survey would miss, and structured workshops turn those values into actual design requirements. Baumann, Van Wynsberghe, and Severs show this already working in real AV workshops, while Tan and Aranda-Muñoz show it holding up in other fields, from social service to healthcare. And it matters: Forlano and Mathew show that the friction a speculative provocation creates, like pushback, confusion or reframing, is exactly where values surface, not a flaw in the method. Still, the method isn't automatic; Barendregt warns that most participatory work only includes experts, not the affected public, which is exactly why running real workshops with pantry users, not just experts, was the right choice.

Author(s): Van Wynsberghe, A., & Guimarães Pereira, Â.
Central claim: This paper argues that autonomous vehicles are being built to solve a different problem than the mobility problem people actually have, and that only participatory speculative workshops with citizens reveal this mismatch, because when citizens imagine their own futures, they redefine mobility on their own terms rather than the industry's.
Gap or limitation: Their participants were largely people who attended EU public-engagement events, so the sample doesn't specifically reach the transport-excluded, service-dependent population (like Arthur) that our project centers on.
Journal or Proceedings: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 9, Article 284
Key concepts or framework:
Futures Making Ateliers: group workshops using Lego, cards, and physical objects to help citizens imagine and prototype alternative mobility futures.
MacGuffin: a device that isn't the real point but sets the story in motion; they argue the AV worked this way, as a prompt that got people imagining alternatives rather than as the actual subject.
Material deliberation: using physical objects in workshops so that non-expert, embodied knowledge gets included in debates usually dominated by experts.
Paper Title: The politics and imaginary of 'autonomous vehicles': A participatory journey.
Quotable moment: "Such engagement activities should play a central role in policy-making involving technological innovations, as these results showcase how participants’ experiences can allow for a variety of outcomes and solutions to be considered without falling prey to technological ‘solutionism’." ("Alternative mobility futures for Europe" section)
Relevance to argument: This paper is both a direct precedent for speculative AV workshops with citizens and a mirror of our core finding since that efficiency-driven industry visions of AVs don't match what communities actually value. It strongly supports our thread: the workshop-plus-speculative-provocation method is precisely what surfaced the gap between the industry's "what AVs are for" and the community's own mobility concerns.

Author(s): Severs, R., Wu, J., Diels, C., Harrow, D., Singleton, J., & Winsor, R.
Central claim: This paper argues that transport-excluded groups hold specific, identifiable design needs for shared autonomous vehicles that mainstream AV design misses, and that participatory workshops are the necessary method for surfacing those needs, since these groups have no direct experience of the technology to draw on otherwise.
Gap or limitation: With only 11 participants across four workshops, and a focus on vehicle interiors rather than the wider service system, it doesn't address how AV deployment reshapes community-level access or governance which is the infrastructure-scale question our argument foregrounds.
Journal or Proceedings: Adjunct Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on Automotive User Interfaces and Interactive Vehicular Applications
Key concepts or framework:
Journey mapping: participants walk through what a typical trip currently looks like for them, exposing where existing mobility breaks down.
Transport exclusion: the framing that certain groups are structurally locked out of mobility, making it a design and equity problem rather than a personal one.
Participatory design activity: hands-on co-design where excluded participants generate their own solutions for a technology they've never used.
Paper Title: Imagining an inclusive future for shared autonomous vehicle interiors: A participatory design workshop study
Quotable moment: "Participatory design was used in the second phase of the work-shops to engage participants in considering future scenarios and developing ideas for how SAVs could be made more inclusive" (2.3 Participatory Design Section)
Relevance to argument: This is the closest paper in terms of method, with the same technology (AVs), same kind of underserved population, same multi-workshop approach with a not-yet-experienced technology. It directly supports our thread by proving the workshop method already produces real, usable design insight with exactly the kind of participants and technology our project involves.

Author(s): Tan, Y., Soh, K.X., Zhang, R., Lee, J., Meng, H., Sen, B., & Lee, Y.-C.
Central claim: This paper argues that a not-yet-embedded technology in a social service setting must be co-designed with frontline practitioners through workshops, because only that process surfaces their real concerns; over lost skills, overreliance, and threats to the human core of the profession; early enough to shape the design.
Gap or limitation: All participants came from two agencies in a single country, and the study is about AI casework tools rather than mobility, so its value for us is in the method and the pattern of practitioner concern, not in the specific technology.
Journal or Proceedings: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA '25)
Key concepts or framework:
Two-stage participatory design: The study’s overarching methodology, Stage 1 being co-design workshops to build a prototype, and Stage 2 including contextual inquiry where practitioners test it on real cases.
Boundary work: the line practitioners draw between "monotonous" administrative labor and the "professional, knowledge-based" work they see as core to their identity, which new tech threatens to cross.
Overreliance: the risk that workers lean on the tool's output without critical checking, especially junior staff.
Paper Title: Empowering social service with AI: Insights from a participatory design study with practitioners.
Quotable moment: The centre director (D1)quoted, "One of our concerns is... [will using this AI] actually dis-able our ability to make assessments?" (Section 4.2.4)
Relevance to argument: This is our strongest domain-matched precedent covering social service, the same context SECS operates in. It supports our thread by showing that workshops with frontline social service workers reliably surface exactly the relational-trust and human-connection concerns that our own Seniors & Volunteers and Stakeholder workshops raised, reinforcing that these values only emerge through participatory methods, not from studying the technology alone.

Author(s): Aranda-Muñoz, Á., Bozic Yams, N., & Carlgren, L.
Central claim: This paper argues that combining speculative design with artistic intervention across a series of workshops actively strengthens participants' sense of agency over their own future, meaning speculative workshops don't just collect opinions, they change participants' relationship to a future being shaped around them.
Gap or limitation: Its institutional setting (a formal training center) is more controlled than a community-based food pantry context, so it doesn't speak to running speculative workshops with an underserved, non-professional population.
Key concepts or framework:
Speculative Design: A practice that uses design not to solve immediate problems, but to create "diegetic prototypes" that open up discourse and allow people to question preferable futures
Design Fiction: A form of speculative design that uses a collection of artifacts to build a fictional world, helping participants explore alternative realities and assess current practices
Experiential futures: futures that participants feel and enact in the moment, rather than discuss in the abstract.
Paper Title: Co-experiential futuring: Where speculative design and arts meet futures studies
Quotable moment: "The core idea behind speculating through design is not to predict and present how things will be or solve a particular problem, but to open up the design situation and discourse so people can discuss and question alternative and preferable futures" (Section 2: Collaborative design futuring and experiential futures)
Relevance to argument: Though not about AVs, this supports our thread by proving the workshop-plus-speculation method reliably works in a completely different domain (healthcare-worker training), which answers the obvious objection that our method only worked because of our specific context. It's our generalizability evidence for choosing workshops over interviews.

Central claim: This paper argues that when a technology isn't yet part of people's everyday lives, the only adequate way to inquire into stakeholders' values is to fuse participatory design with design fiction, because neither studying current practice nor speculation alone can surface values about a technology that doesn't yet exist.
Gap or limitation: Its own case study is very small (six volunteers and one short workshop), so it offers a well-argued rationale for the method but only preliminary evidence that it works at scale.
Key concepts or framework:
Value Sensitive Design (VSD): an established HCI approach for accounting for human values throughout the design process, not just performance and usability.
Participatory Design Fictions (PDF): their core framework: a method for soliciting stakeholder input through "strategically incomplete fictions", stories that establish a setting and characters but end prematurely at a critical decision point.
Grounded Theory: A qualitative analysis method used to identify conceptual categories and value themes within the collected stories
Paper Title: Enabling value sensitive AI systems through participatory design fictions
Quotable moment: "PD thus embodies moral commitments to diverse human values, meanwhile a more descriptive, bottom-up approach to integrate them in technology design." (Participatory Design Section)
Relevance to argument: This is the paper that names and justifies our exact method, just applied to AI rather than AVs - we could not interview pantry users about a non-existent AV, so we did what this paper prescribes: brought in real stakeholders and gave them a speculative version to react to. It is our direct answer to "why not just run interviews."

Author(s): Barendregt, L., Bendor, R., & van Eekelen, B.F.
Central claim: This paper argues that participatory futuring, despite its democratic rhetoric, mostly includes only experts and professionals rather than affected publics, and that even when publics are involved the process is often not designed to genuinely empower them.
Gap or limitation: As a review of published academic work, it captures only what has been formally written up, missing informal or community-led engagement that never reached publication.
Key concepts or framework:
Participatory futuring: collective activities in which people imagine and deliberate over possible futures.
Arnstein's ladder of citizen participation: a classic scale of how much real power participants hold, from token consultation to genuine control; they argue futuring can empower in ways this ladder misses.
The 'subject of the future': an identity position that could make participation more generative, by casting participants as authors of the future rather than data sources.
Paper Title: Public participation in futuring: A systematic literature review.
Quotable moment: "While establishing the scope of our study we found that much participatory futuring is only inclusive of experts and professionals, and during the study we found that a majority of participatory futuring with publics involves them alongside people participating in an expert or professional capacity." (Section 6.1, "How inclusive?")
Relevance to argument: This review supplies field-level evidence that our project's decision to include pantry users and volunteers directly, not only SECS staff or experts, is a genuinely stronger and less common move, which backs our "passive users vs stakeholders" sub-point with more than opinion. It positions our participatory choice as filling a documented gap in the field.

Central claim: This paper argues that combining speculative and participatory design for urban technology should aim for "friction"; deliberate moments of disagreement, resistance, and reframing among stakeholders; because it is precisely in that friction that people's embedded values become visible and contestable.
Gap or limitation: Its stakeholders are mixed policy actors rather than a specifically underserved community, so it doesn't address the power asymmetries between participant types that a food-pantry context makes central.
Key concepts or framework:
Design friction: deliberately built-in resistance or disagreement in a design process, treated as productive rather than as a failure.
Participatory Workshops: A series of five-hour workshops where participants used design fiction to move past today's technical constraints and focus on human values.
Designing Policy Toolkit: A large-format visual poster that serves as a "boundary object" to bridge the gap between scientific experts, policymakers, and citizens. It explains concepts like value-sensitive design and provides a methodology for collaborative workshops.
Paper Title: From design fiction to design friction: Speculative and participatory design of values-embedded urban technology.
Quotable moment: "this paper introduces the term design friction to capture a range of examples of the ways in which tension, conflict, or disagreement allowed for the discussion of urban tech-nology to move out of the “black box” and into prototyping alternative possible futures and questions rather than problem solving for today’s challenges." (Conclusion Section)
Relevance to argument: This gives a name and a rationale to the "breakdown moments" in our own workshops, like the points where our speculative AV concept met resistance, confusion, or reframing. It supports our thread by reframing that friction not as a flaw in the method but as the exact mechanism through which community values (and their misalignment with efficiency logic) surface.

Central claim: This paper argues that a single believable speculative prototype, even a fake but plausible product website, can function as a public-facing tool that provokes people into reflecting on their own values around an emerging technology, rather than merely eliciting their opinion of a product.
Gap or limitation: It's a single design case with no formal participant study attached, so it can't tell us how reactions were gathered or how the method holds up with a real, diverse community.
Key concepts or framework:
Diegetic prototype: a fictional artifact built to feel like it belongs to a real, believable world (borrowed from Kirby's film-studies concept).
Value Elicitation: using the prototype specifically to surface concerns like privacy, autonomy, and control, not usability.
Speculative Realism: treating design as inquiry that expands what's imaginable rather than solving a predefined problem.
Paper Title: Design futuring through diegetic prototypes: Provoking value reflection on emerging technologies.
Quotable moment: "We need infrastructures for value reflection - spaces where people can meaningfully examine not just technologies, but the human values being reinforced, challenged, or eroded. Diegetic prototypes, when paired with thoughtful facilitation, offer one such infrastructure." (Ch.6 - Conclusion)
Relevance to argument: This paper isolates the specific mechanism our other sources only imply, that is - how a speculative artifact pulls values out of people, which directly justifies our decision to build a speculative AV provocation rather than survey or interview participants. It's less direct (a single case study, no community workshop), but it names the engine that makes our provocation work.

Author(s): Sörries, P., Leimstädtner, D., & Müller-Birn, C.
Central claim: This paper argues that a structured, multi-phase participatory workshop can reliably convert vulnerable stakeholders' stated values into concrete design requirements, demonstrating that value elicitation through workshops produces actionable design direction rather than just discussion.
Gap or limitation: Only three workshops in a single healthcare and legal context (GDPR-bound Germany), so the four-phase method's transferability to a mobility or food-pantry setting is untested.
Journal or Proceedings: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 8(CSCW1), Article 16.
Key concepts or framework:
Participatory Value Elicitation: a four-phase workshop method built specifically to draw out and then translate participants' values into requirements.
Value Sensitive Design (VSD): the same foundational values-in-design framework Liao & Muller build on, here operationalized in a real workshop.
Reflective Design: deliberately surfacing the usually-unconscious values a technology carries by having participants reflect on alternatives.
Paper Title: Advocating values through meaningful participation: Introducing a method to elicit and analyze values for enriching data donation practices in healthcare.
Quotable moment: "Finally, we emphasize that our workshop concept enabled participants to recognize the ambivalence of values" & "In other words, values illuminate personal experiences and are closely linked to them, thus offering valuable insights for technology design." (Section 5.2 Reflections on the Suitability of our Method)
Relevance to argument: This is the clearest evidence on our list that the workshop-to-values-to-design pipeline actually closes; that values surfaced in workshops become real design requirements, not just talk. It directly supports our thread's implicit promise: that the community concerns our workshops surfaced (equitable access, relational trust, flexibility) can concretely inform how AV-related infrastructure should be designed.

Author(s): Wong, R.Y., Mulligan, D.K., Van Wyk, E., Pierce, J., & Chuang, J.
Central claim: This paper argues that a workbook of speculative design fictions can serve as a deliberate "values lever" that surfaces people's underlying social values about an emerging technology, meaning speculative artifacts are an active tool for eliciting values, not just a passive stimulus to react to.
Gap or limitation: Participants were an expert population (graduate students training as tech professionals), not an underserved community, so we can't assume the workbook effect transfers identically to food pantry users without adaptation.
Journal or Proceedings: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 1(CSCW), Article 111.
Key concepts or framework:
Speculative Design Workbook: a collection of speculative design proposals assembled to help people explore and reflect on a design space, not to pitch a real product.
Values levers (from Shilton): anything that shifts a conversation to foreground values and treat them as central to design; they argue their workbooks acted as one.
Privacy By Design (PBD): embedding privacy protections into products during design, ratherthan retroactively
Paper Title: Eliciting values reflections by engaging privacy futures using design workbooks.
Quotable moment: "Critical, speculative, and value-centered design approaches can be used to elicit reflections on relevant social values early in product development" (Abstract Section)
Relevance to argument: This is our strongest, award-winning proof that a speculative artifact deliberately elicits values rather than merely provoking a reaction, which is the precise justification for why we built a speculative AV provocation instead of asking participants directly. It anchors the "why this method" core of our thread.
